summary: OEM, New Old Stock, great value.
reviewText_clean: The drive I received is a WD Western Digital Blue 320GB / WD3200KS / 16MB buffer / Manufactured in Jan 30 2010. The description spec'd this as having a 8MB buffer so the 16MB buffer was a pleasant surprise. I confirmed this is a true OEM drive on the WD website. WD does not warranty OEM products so the warranty comes from the re-seller. The drive arrived sealed in the factory anti-static bag inside a standard OEM carrier. The packing was professional grade, the carrier consists of a cardboard box with two plastic inserts to protect and cushion the drive. See picture. My drive passed the Western Digital short and long tests with no errors. It also executed a zero write with no errors. The drive has no bad sectors. It is in perfect working condition. I suggest you take the time to long scan your drive and zero write it when you receive it to insure it works properly. The Data Lifeguard software to do this is free on the WD website. Scans like this will take a little time but this is the only way to know your drive is reliable. This model is several years old so it's read an write speeds are not impressive by today's standards. The sequential R/W topped out at about 60MB/s while random R/W was about 2MB/s. This drive will seem sluggish next to today's models and like a turtle next to a modern SSD. Even today there is a place for drives of this speed. The drive is well suited for long term file storage, repairing an older machine, use in an external USB case, or for use in a DVR. Personally I use this type of drive to store backup images and it works great for this purpose. So to sum it up... This drive is an OEM New Old Stock item. It came professionally packaged and passed all the tests when it arrived. It's definitely not fast but it a good value if you know what you are buying. I would buy it again and I would recommend it to a friend.

summary: It Worked for a little while
reviewText_clean: I purchased this laptop 15 months ago. It came with a free upgrade to Windows 10, which I downloaded and it ran flawlessly (technically) until 2 days ago. That story later. I did not like Windows 10 but Win 8.1 was equally annoying until I learned that I would make it appear like a Win 7 machine with traditional desktop icons and could largely ignore the Windows 10 structure. However I discovered a very annoying aspect of this particular laptop. The keyboard is not standard either in key spacing or in which keys were adjacent to each other, and because I am a very fast touch typist I discovered that emails would send before I was ready, the cursor would go to odd places and then delete lines, and it had to do with key spacing and placement. This week I gave up on it because I lost too many paragraphs, emails and documents--and decided to go back to my 2011 Lenovo Thinkpad. Now the second part of the story that makes me conclude never again with an ASUS. I took out all my documents, photos, music, etc., and put it onto backup media (two different backup systems) and then followed Microsoft instructions for a reset to clean condition before I gave it to a college student who had use for a good laptop. I was given several options, one was to reset (which I chose) and then whether to keep my data or do a clean install (which I chose). Partly through the reset process it told me that there was a failure and asked whether I wanted to try again. I selected try again. It got well through the process when it recycled and then stopped and gave an error message: boot drive inaccessible. Now the laptop restarts, stops and restarts again, only getting as far as the splash screen ASUS IN SEARCH OF INCREDIBLE. It does this endlessly. I went to Microsoft and got instructions for a windows repair utility and a new copy of Windows10. It initially opened the bios but I could see very little to change except to set boot order to start with my PNY flash drive then save and exit and nothing happened. With the flash drive inserted into the USB it continues to just recycle the splash screen. So I sent an email to support at ASUS, noting that there were lots of comments about a similar thing happening to other laptops when they tried to reset them but that the experts who responded with help about what to do were way over my head in what was necessary. I got a reply from ASUS support that said it appeared to be a drive failure and to send it to ASUS and because it was now out of warranty (barely) the minimum cost to repair it would be $510. Seriously? I do not think it is a drive failure, I think it needs some tinkering with the bios that is beyond my willing to try so I will take it to a local computer shop tomorrow. All this for a computer that I am going to give away because I think it is a very badly designed product. UPDATE AUGUST 10: I took the laptop to a local computer repair facility that I trust. They confirmed that it was a problem between ASUS and MICROSOFT that is encountered during a clean install and while I don't fully understand the issue, it has to do with the way the "reset" option works, so that if the clean install option is selected the ASUS fails. The repair shop was able to fix whatever went wrong for a $129 repair bill and I now have a clean install on the computer. This was a very bad experience, and if I was not as careful a user with multiple backups I would have lost everything on my laptop. BE WARNED.

I was watching Netflix, wasn't playing a game or doing anything hardware intensive and it just shut off. I attempted to turn the computer back on and nothing happened. I saw some smoke coming out of the back of my case so I removed the side panel and smoke ended up billowing out of the case. I unplugged everything and waited a few minutes then took a look inside and there are burn marks all over the unit. I can only assume it short circuited since there is quite literally no other explanation, but luckily it doesn't seem to have taken any of my other components down with it except the motherboard which had it's PCI slot fried (GPU still works though). This unit is SUPPOSED to come with a warranty but after sending an email to the manufacturer I found out that my unit is in fact NOT covered under warranty. Keep in mind, this was just my experience with it but I would double check your warranty status just to be sure. I don't want to say that it will happen to everyone, your mileage may vary but my computer just randomly shut off while I was using it. I was watching Netflix, wasn't playing a game or doing anything hardware intensive and it just shut off. I attempted to turn the computer back on and nothing happened. I saw some smoke coming out of the back of my case so I removed the side panel and smoke ended up billowing out of the case. I unplugged everything and waited a few minutes then took a look inside and there are burn marks all over the unit. I can only assume it short circuited since there is quite literally no other explanation, but luckily it doesn't seem to have taken any of my other components down with it except the motherboard which had it's PCI slot fried (GPU still works though). This unit is SUPPOSED to come with a warranty but after sending an email to the manufacturer I found out that my unit is in fact NOT covered under warranty. My motherboard is older and the warranty has already expired so I now have to pay out of pocket for another motherboard and a new power supply. Keep in mind, this was just my experience with it but I would double check your warranty status just to be sure. I gave it four stars because while it was working, it did what it was supposed to do and I never had a problem out of it. Had all the cables I needed, has all the cables needed for an SLI/Crossfire gaming rig, the cords are the appropriate length, maybe even a little too long for my liking. I'm taking away a star because of the unit dying on me, seemingly out of nowhere, and the lack of proper warranty support.

summary: Works well under Windows 7
reviewText_clean: I bought this in order to try and update the firmware on my Samsung 840 EVO mSATA drive. The adapter is simple, and it was easy to install the 840 in the mSATA socket and clip it down. I plugged it into the native SATA on my ASUS motherboard. The boot drive for that machine is a Samsung 840 EVO SATA. The mSATA was plugged into the same Intel disk controller as the SATA drive. Samsung Magician (latest version as of early April 2016) under Windows 7 Pro 64-bit detected the drive just fine, but claimed the firmware version was the latest. It correctly identified the firmware version, but he version on the website was newer by 2 revisions. I had used the same PC and Magician to update the firmware on the SATA drive. The firmware versions for the 840 EVO SATA and mSATA are unique - different version numbers. So I downloaded the ISO Linux-based updater, and attempted to update with it. It generated some kind of error, and exited. I contacted Samsung, described what I had done, and they blamed the Syba adapter, saying it had 'an incompatible controller'. I do not actually believe this, as there is no sign of any kind of disk controller chip (or any digital chip, for that matter) on the Syba board. It seems to be a form-factor adapter, with a couple of analog bits, and little else besides the mSATA socket. So, inconclusive. It works fine under Windows. I benchmarked it, and performance between the mSATAwith the Syba and the SATA were similar. But - Big Props to Samsung on their handling of the firmware issue. Someone answered the phone immediately (and they spoke perfect, native English), they understood all the technical information that I provided, and willingly set up an exchange. They sent me a pre-paid overnight label for UPS, and had the thing back (the original drive, actually, just updated properly) in three days. The E-Mail communication was top-notch. Samsung knocks it out of the park, warranty-wise, unlike Crucial. Crucial's tech support and warranty support is abysmal - worst I have seen in many years. I found this out due to a failure of an M4 drive that my Dad bought. Meanwhile, I have owned multiple Samsung SSDs, and zero problems. The firmware on the mSATA was an issue, but the manner in which they resolved the problem exceeded expectations.

reviewText_clean: The seller did a great job fulfilling the order. It arrived ahead of time, the order was accurate, the packaging was fantastic, and the products were in great condition (I ordered it new). This negative review rests solely on Microsoft. About 6 months later, the keyboard stopped working. I saw I had a year warranty on the computer, so I wasn't worried. After months of navigating different sites for Microsoft, I finally stumbled on an area within my office 365 online account where I could register devices for service. On May 7, 2017, I attempted to register the device for warranty service and Microsoft finally recognizes the device , but says it's out of warranty. I purchased it July 14, 2016. A little after 4 2/3 months, the left headphone stopped putting out sound. Since there is a 12 month warranty on these, I contacted SOUNDPeats Customer Support. Service has been TERRIBLE. I've been told I can return them. On my own dime. But I can't get a return address out of the CS rep. I also can't get an answer about how I'm supposed to get a new pair or how they will reimburse me should I just buy them. SO...TERRIBLE CUSTOMER SERVICE. That 12-month warranty is worth jack. summary: 2016 unit eliminates the issues of my 2014 unit
reviewText_clean: UPDATE: December 2016 This unit is used to receive and record OTA digital TV programs. It can be useful as a receiver in those instances when video equipment, such as a DVD recorder, does not have a built-in tuner. As a recorder, one attaches either a USB stick or external HDD (the HDD yields much better video quality and playback); it has both RCA and HDMI outputs. It records in *.mts format which does not play nice with PC viewers, e. g., VLC, at least in my system. (Playback is flawless through the HW-150PVR, though). I convert the *.mts files to MP4 to store and/or playback on my PC or tablet. The EPG capability is a bit limited, yielding a a day or two at most. However, one does not need the EPG display to record programs, i.e., if one knows the date and time of a program, the unit can be programmed to record that program no matter when it airs. I originally purchased the HW-150PVR in January 2014; it died in October 2016, exhibiting various hiccups along the way. In spite of its somewhat short life, I purchased two more HW-150PVRs in November and am in the process of purchasing another. Why? For one reason: in addition to my antenna signal booster, these units boost my weak signal even further, minimizing degraded signals (I am 100 miles from the nearest broadcasting city); secondly, unlike my DVD recorder, these units record HD quality video regardless of the recording time; thirdly, recording is easy: press the remote record button and unit starts recording within ten seconds. Speaking of the DVD recorder, my recorder (  Panasonic DMR-EA18K Tunerless 1080p Upconverting DVD Recorder  ) does not have a tuner so I also use the HW-150DVR to feed TV signals to it. The resultant recordings are flawless. Originally, I gave the HW-150PVR a low rating because of the various hiccups I experienced and its short life (January 2014 to October 2016). I do not know if the current unit has been upgraded but compared to that which I purchased in 2014, the current unit is more responsive and, to date, lacks the hiccups I previously noted. Given the apparent improvements, I suspect that my original unit may have been defective - which happens. The HW-150PVR provides excellent quality, conveniently made recordings. I would also note that, subsequent to my purchase, Mediasonic sent me an email urging me to avail myself of their "100% Customer Satisfaction Guarantee" should I experience any issues. Given their support, I purchased a third unit and feel very comfortably doing so. Ed

summary: Caught fire after just over 3 months! Are you kidding me? Toshiba Won't Replace it!.
reviewText_clean: I've been building computers for 20 years and I've never had this happen before. I'm stunned. The fire got so hot a couple pins burned right off. I have an EVGA 220-G2-0750-XR 80 PLUS GOLD 750W PSU (the best quality you can buy IMO) and lost one of the Sata power cables as well because the fire (which began somewhere inside the inner connection of the hard drive) melted the sata cable connector and ruined the wiring in it. The flame also reached my WD drive below it but it appears still intact though it's scorched on the outside (running tests on it as I write this). My Samsung was not so lucky as I lost 15 years of work on it! I got the Toshiba in order to back up the Samsung in the first place. Well, never got the chance to back up everything. Because my case can be quickly be opened I was able to stop it from spreading any further at least. My PC now smells like soot. I have a lot of pets and roommates and this could have turned into a deadly house fire if I hadn't been sitting next to my pc at the time. This put us in physical danger. What a nightmare. I'm beside myself with anger. Edit (2/16/2016): I just tried to go through the Warranty process but Toshiba does not offer replacements for this hard drive. Instead they want me to take a store credit toward the purchase of a completely different drive that can ONLY be purchased from their Website. The only thing they carry with the same capacity is a badly-rated EXTERNAL HD. They don't even carry the "newer" model Amazon links to above. I just can't rely on Toshiba keeping it's promises to honor their warranties. Contrast this to EVGA who sent me a BRAND NEW replacement PSU when I asked them about the possibility of a short in the sata cable which had gotten melted by the fire. (They were adamant that the hard drive itself would have been the source of the short. Considering the quality of their hardware I'm inclined to believe them. Edit (2/21/2016): Contacted Amazon support (name was Niel) and he did me a solid and replaced the hard drive. Well, the male power sata connector on the replacement came completely lose the first time I unplugged my sata power cable. Never had that happen with any hard drive and I've had so many over the years. So I have to assume there is a serious manufacturing flaw in the Toshiba Sata Power ports. So, embarrassed to even ask, I contact Amazon support again and without hesitation the support person, Sheshadri, apologized and put in another replacement. Quite astounded at how generous Amazon has been to me. The 2nd replacement arrived today and I'm going to video record the installation (definitely going to test the integrity of the sata power connector in the process). I hope the first 2 were just a fluke. If not, there's this lawyer I saw on TV.... :p

summary: Easy Installation, Great Sound
reviewText_clean: I installed this in my 2007 Toyota Avalon XLS with navigation and JBL Stereo. So far it has been great. I set it for satellite radio emulation, which allows me to change tracks and answer and end phone calls using the steering wheel buttons. It comes with a y-splitter cable so that you don't lose the functionality of the AM radio that shares a port on the back of the radio with where the satellite radio would be. According to the manual, there is an additional splitter that can be purchased to retain any satellite radio functions along with this module and AM radio, but I did not need this for my installation. The sound is crystal clear. The module connects automatically, and mine was already set not to have the announcement about the Bluetooth connecting. Installation on this particular car was straight forward. I followed an installation kit video on YouTube for a different module, specifically the GTA Pure Bluetooth Kit that is specific to my vehicle. With just a few pry tools and a 10 millimeter ratchet with extension, I had this installed in about 30 minutes. This kit pair nicely with this USB and aux extension: Xtenzi USB & 3.5mm AUX extension Flush Mount 2 Meter Cable , 1/8 AUX Car Bike Boat Motercycle Lead. I removed the center console from my car and drilled a hole using this stepper bit: Neiko 10189A Titanium Step Drill Bit, High Speed Steel | 7/16" to 1-1/8" | Total 12 Step Sizes. In order to fit the plug, I had to drill down to the next to last step on the stepper bit. Just go slowly, and you shouldn't crack the plastic. Removing the entire center console was fairly straightforward. There are two Phillips head screws under the trim that has to be popped off to place the unit under the cup holders and next to the shifter. In the larger, farther back compartment, there are two bolts under the carpeting inside the compartment. Once those four are removed, simply lift and undo the wiring that power the cigarette lighters. I drilled the hole for the port in the smaller compartment and removed the cell phone holder. The whole assembly works great so far. I will update it if something happens to change that. I am concerned about the fact that USA Spec may not offer any tech support, so I purchased a Square Trade warranty. Hopefully I don't have to use it.

summary: My new best bud(s), I will buy more, I can't believe I'm listening to ...Bluetooth...earbuds...might work with your Kindle Fire
reviewText_clean: I think my review title kind of says it all...I LOVE THESE BUDS! When it comes Bluetooth earbuds, I have tried a lot and one thing I have learned is the sound quality is only half the battle. Earbuds require a good fit for the best sound quality, unlike over-the-ear headphones which have much larger tolerances when it comes to fit, really almost none at all as long as they cover your ears. I have tried earbuds that cost several times more than these and had relatively good reviews but for me the sound quality was terrible because they did not fit my ears properly and it had nothing to do with the size of eargels I used. I have tried earbuds where the design itself prevented me from even getting the buds in my ear canal properly. If these fit you properly, trust me, you have found your Bluetooth earbud nirvana. One thing I keep having to remind myself about these is that I am using ... Bluetooth... earbuds... ... amazing, Bluetooth ... earbuds... ... amazing... The sound quality falls in between standard resolution and high resolution, they call it HD, stands for high definition I suppose all I know is that it is pretty close to high resolution for...Bluetooth...earbuds... ... amazing... I guarantee you will not find better sound quality for the price of these, IF they fit you properly. I really hope they will fit you well, the sound quality is so good it's worth the try. The only reason I took a star off was for other things that had nothing to do with the sound quality. First was the earwings are very soft and I really wonder how much they help, most earbuds I use have a semi-rigid earwing that uses a friction hold, these would have a very minimal friction hold. I have had them pop out a couple times while walking, I'm pretty sure most of my hold is coming from the tight fit of the eargels. The little blue LED is a little annoying if you are in the dark with your eyes closed because of the intermittent flashing. Another thing to remember is these are designed to work with Android and Apple devices. They are not designed to work with the Kindle Fire or at least they are not supposed to work with Kindle Fire. When I first got mine the first device I used them with was my Kindle Fire HD 8.9, the sound was I can only describe as "gooey" and it skipped a couple times a song. When I contacted Motorola about it that is when I was told they were not designed to work with the Kindle Fire. Well guess what they do. For some reason the sound has gotten better and you could almost say it is better than on my Android phone, the volume is definitely louder on the Kindle Fire and now I don't get any skips either. For the size of these the battery life is absolutely phenomenal, and the little voice will tell you each time you connect how much battery life in hours you have left. Not only do I plan to buy more for friends and family I plan to buy another pair for myself just to have a spare. I guess you can tell I like these buds despite the issues I had. Give them a try, if you get a nice tight fit I guarantee you will love them and remember you are listening to...Bluetooth...earbuds... ...amazing... Update You should be getting good sound quality if not try pushing them a little farther in your ear canal, if it is uncomfortable try a smaller ear gel if possible. The sound quality can be dramatically different depending on how far you can get them in your ear canal. The sound quality is noticeably better than standard resolution and you should be able to hear it. Also as I and others have mentioned the sound quality does seem to improve over time in some situations. This seems to be pretty much the norm for many Bluetooth devices and one that I have experienced the majority of the times myself. Also I'm easily getting the 9 hours battery life that is advertised so I don't know if high volumes might have a significantly faster drain although it should not be that much. The voice will also say I have 9 hours of play time when I have a full charge and will tell me how much each time I connect as the battery drains so if your voice is not saying you have 9 hours when fully charged then it might be an issue with how you are charging the buds. By the way, I just wanted to add that I apologize these are being sold for full retail right now. Before I wrote my review they were selling for $65, I am not joking as soon as I wrote and posted my review saying I was going to buy more they raised the price, that was over a week ago. Ok, maybe it was just a coincidence. :)

summary: ATH-MX50 plus FiiO A3 amp, match made in heaven  - BEST DEAL to boot - these are great headphones
reviewText_clean: I could imagine, like most people, you've been shopping around for quite some time for headphones...right? I think I spent a good month + digging through websites, Amazon reviews, YouTube vids, techie article after article to see the best headphones without dropping a fortune. My budget was to stay under $200. That limits me to a select few....and the ones I found were the V-Moda's and the Audio Technica ATH-M50X's. Let me say that I could not be more pleased with my purchase. And to boot, this was an awesome deal. I had not even considered an amp when I first considered looking into headphones, but what a win to find this deal. ALL for $149...I was actually hesitant thinking that this deal was too good to be true....I think I was correct...it's even better. This combo is even better than I could have hoped. Let me start off by saying that there is a reason that the M50X's have been the highest rated, year after year. The sound quality is phenomenal...clear, crisp. Snappy bass, clear highs...actually listening to most of my music catalog like never before. I listen to a broad range of music genre, and yet to find anything that doesn't sound excellent with these cans. Now, an additional plus...the FiiO A3 amp...this thing rocks. It boosts so well and clean..I can normally only listed about half volume with the A3 on "high" until it just gets too loud. However, the music is still not distorted...again the M50X's can handle everything that I've been able to throw at them. The additional added plus, they travel well. I was a bit worried that I would be lugging around this massive set of headphones or look goofy while on a plane with these strapped to my head. Not the case, they fit really well, are VERY comfortable...in fact fall asleep several times with them on, forget that they are on my head...so after hours of listening, taking them off, you don't get that "blood rushing back to my ear" pain. These travel very well also - great on plane and I have yet to have another set of headphones that could compare. I was also a bit hesitant because they are "plastic-y" and have a bit of a cheap look being all plastic. But not so...they feel solid...don't feel cheap or poorly constructed. Overall, these are just great / awesome headphones. A couple of other additional items I also picked up from Amazon that work well with this combo is a good case and a good set of aux cables...would suggest to pick up a 4ft set with standard 3.5mm jacks. The small jack that is included that comes with the FiiO A3 is a bit clumsy because it's very small / short. It's designed to connect straight to the device and comes with a couple of bands to hold the amp to your player or phone / device. I opted just to get a nice 4ft aux cable. You have to be mindful of shutting off the power button...which is also doubles as the volume button on the A3 amp (nice to have this functionality on hand also!!!). If you leave on, the charge will drain. You can listed while plugged in...I hear no white noise while the amp is plugged in, but some people have noted on other versions of FiiO amplifiers they detect white noise in background....but I've yet to hear anything. Everything came in SEALED factory boxes, all with sealed warranty cards (both headphones and the amp) - all new, legit, functional, and worth every $$$. I would certainly buy this setup again and would recommend this to anyone interested in new headphones. I love them...in fact listening to them while I write this...A++

summary: Compact speaker with great sound
reviewText_clean: When I first saw the SoundCore Sport, I was skeptical about how well a small speaker would perform in terms of sound quality and volume. After using it for several hours, I am really impressed with every aspect of this device. Included in the cardboard packing is the speaker itself, a Micro USB charging cable, and a silicone wrist strap, which is quite small. You can use an AUX cable to play music, but no cable is included. The speaker is very compact, so you could carry it around with the wrist strap on when walking. It only weighs 224g according to my scales, too, so it shouldn't take up much room or weight in a backpack. Usually smaller speakers make sacrifices in other areas, but I would not say that is the case here. The speaker is louder than some of my larger speakers, and certainly loud enough to fill a large room. The sound is crisp, with all areas of the soundstage audible. It did not sound tinny due to its size and I was really impressed with it. This SoundCore Sport is said to be waterproof, and my tests have confirmed that. I submerged this for around a minute in my sink, and it was able to play music in the water - obviously the music was distorted, but the speaker was fine. This would make for a really good shower speaker, as splashes do not matter. The battery life is advertised at 10 hours, so you can go a day without charging it, and probably have some battery left - impressive for such a compact speaker. Along the top edge are four buttons - on, volume up and down, and a multifunction pause/skip track/pair button. A microphone for calls is also built into the unit. Overall, I cannot fault this speaker. The sound is much better than you would expect for the size, and that is combined with good battery life and a rugged waterproof design. It is also backed up by Anker's 18-month warranty. Highly recommended. Note: I was sent a free review unit by the seller, but the opinions expressed in this review are my own.

reviewText_clean: [Reviewed by my son, Chris.] This monitor is being used in my home office, where it sees home-office tasks most of the time, and some gaming when those tasks are done. The home office PC is a dull and practical four-door-sedan of a machine running Windows 10, with a GeForce GT430 card. Unboxing was no problem. The monitor was bagged and sandwiched between the familiar foam clamshells. Also in the box, a circular base, a 6 inch tall stand, three cables, and manuals/compliance/warranty/safety docs. I didn't look at those. Setup was simple: stand attaches to base with a single lockscrew (no screwdriver needed), and slots into back of monitor. One cord for power (actually a small transformer brick and two cords) and one HDMI cord. Plug those in to the usual places and hey presto. About HDMI, actually, that's it. The monitor has two HDMI inputs, a power switch, and a place to plug the power cord. If you've an older video card with only DVI out, you'll want to deal with that. Performance? What can I say. It looks good. Defaults to 1920x1080. I've been editing documents and browsing the web for a few hours now and text is clean, high contrast, and clear. I can't really put it through its paces properly, but I did fire up a little Tropico and it looked great. Any limitations are due to the video card, I think. I watched a few video clips with action scenes in them, and those seemed fine. Shadows seem to keep some detail. Big transitions in brightness seem smooth enough. It looks good: clean, sleek, and simple. At 32", it's noticeably lighter than the 22" monitor that it replaced. I'm happy with it.

summary: GREAT SPEAKER, SOUND AND PRICE
reviewText_clean: I just received this speaker and wanted to say what a GREAT SPEAKER it is for the price. I'll start off by saying it is very well built with the rubberized coating and the form factor (size) is perfect for putting it in your back pack or just carrying it to the beach etc. The sound is excellent with decent "highs" and very rich and deep sound. While I haven't tested the battery yet (rated at 520mAh) ,I'm sure it will be great. I tested this speaker against several other waterproof speakers and here is my "opinion". While everybody has different opinions on how they like their "sound", overall I feel this speaker produces the best sound for the money. You throw in the construction of the speaker and the battery life and you have a great speaker. -Ecoxgear Eco Stone speaker- This is a great speaker as I have owned it for several years. It's waterproof with great battery life (only 2800mAH) and the sound is almost as good as the Anker Souncore Sport XL. However, the Anker speaker has a little more deeper tone to the sound. That doesn't mean it has more bass, it just sounds deeper. -Sharkk O2 and Commando speakers-I had both of these and sent them back. They received great reviews but the sound was not that good. Both came across as "tinny" with it sounding like it was in a concert hall with a slight echo. The Anker Soundcore Sport XL is 10 times better sounding that the Sharkk and the Anker has a bigger battery. -UE Boom 1- Another great sounding speaker that was almost as good as the Anker but again, it didn't produce that rich "deep" sound . This speaker produces a 360 sound because of it's cylinder shape but I don't think the battery is as good as the Anker's battery. eat sounding, water proof Overall, I am very happy with the construction (ruggedness), sound and battery life of this speaker although I haven't tested the battery yet. (Just going on the 5200mAh rating of the battery.) Plus, you throw in an 18 month warranty and great Anker support and you can't go wrong with this speaker. I would highly recommend buying this speaker if you're look for a great sounding, waterproof speaker. I bought this speaker at full price and did not receive anything for the review. (However, if ANKER wants to send me a free one, I'll take it! LOL) One more thing reference the "Bluetooth" of this speaker. It's rated at 66 feet and I haven't tested that yet. However, it seems to be very good as I can have my phone in one room and the speaker in another and it doesn't lose the BT connection. Come on, does anybody really care if it goes 66 feet? The BT is excellent on this speaker.

summary: I swear by Anker products and service
reviewText_clean: What to say? First off, I had no trouble following the directions and installing the screen protector on my new iPad Pro. I love the hinge method Anker uses it makes it so easy to position the glass precisely on the screen. No major bubbles encountered and I was able to remove the 1-2 small ones with the squeegee card. I lost no touch sensitivity due to the screen protector and the Retina display came through bright & clear. I've owned and used this screen protector now for about a year. Sometime in that period something nicked the edge of the glass. Maybe I dropped the stylus I don't know I didn't notice when it happened. I keep the iPad in a case so it had to be open and in use when the nick occurred since it happened on the hinge side of the case. At first I thought there was a hair on the glass & I tried to brush it off it didn't move. I eventually realized that the screen protector had actually cracked from side-to-side and I could see a small nick on the edge at one end of the crack. The crack was barely visible and didn't interfere with using the iPad at all so I didn't think much about it. After months of usage, the two pieces of the protector must have moved slightly because the crack became more visibly noticeable (but the usage was still not impacted). Late last night (Friday night), before I went to bed, I contacted the seller, Anker, and asked if the lifetime guarantee covered that sort of damage. I provided a couple of images of the crack. This morning (Saturday) there was a response in my inbox. I don't know where in the world Anker's customer service is located but I was surprised (and impressed) to get a response on a weekend. They were sorry I'd had a negative experience with the protector and would I please verify my address so they could send me a new one at no charge. Are these guys living in some sort of time warp where customer service is still king or what? I'm old enough to remember those days. I bought my first Anker product 5 years ago and have been a regular customer ever since. I was telling someone just last week that when I need anything for my phone, tablet or computer, I check to see if Anker makes one. The quality of the product has always been top-notch and the customer service superlative. These guys are the best! Don't ever change, Anker!

summary: Judge for yourself - Disfunctional Company or Scam?
reviewText_clean: Tivo in the past has produced equipment that lasted for years and built a fan base accordingly. In recent times Roku, among others, has eroded the customer base for Tivo and placed it's existence in doubt. (note the recent sale of the company) Read this to learn about what I see as a Tivo corporate scam. Tivo: before you call out your legal dogs, this is just my opinion...one I am allowed under the old system. (freedom of speech) It is my belief that to stop the monetary bleeding the following scheme has been implemented: 1) Produce an inferior product subject to early failure. (plenty of evidence to support that reality) 2. Offer a warranty that is very short (realistically 90 days) with major costs passed on to the purchaser after 90 days. 3) Tie this warranty to a long term programming service purchase THAT CANNOT BE TRANSFERRED to a replacement device. 4) Make the "lifetime service" apply to the device rather than the lifetime of the purchaser. It's in the fine print if you have the time and determination to find it. Tivo is banking on most people not spending the time to uncover these conditions that would likely be unacceptable if known. 5) Have Tivo CS agents make claims as difficult as possible to process. I don't feel that a "new" product is manufactured using anything but new parts. Sounds like a salvage company to me. There are other "gotchas", but if you haven't been convinced by now, you really don't need more. Hope this will help others avoid my experience with Tivo.

summary: Bose QC35 vs budget ANC headsets Dylan QS1 and Paww Wavesound 3
reviewText_clean: Recently I went on search for noise cancelling Bluetooth headphones to use while travelling, and also while using noisy outdoor power equipment. My criteria were simple- reliable wireless performance, all day comfort, extended battery life, and high quality sound. Though I am not an audiophile snob, I have been buying and enjoying high end stereo products since the early 1980s, and I understand and enjoy high end sound. For that reason I eliminated the trendy and costly but sonically horrid Beats line and focused on the three models you see here. I broke the review down into sections, so that you can focus on whatever categories mean the most to you. First up is comfort: The Bose QC35 weighed 8.3 oz (235 Grams). They are the lightest in the test, but their outstanding comfort is due to more than just reduced mass. Everything about these headphones is comfortable, including fit, adjustability, and clamping force. They just slip on your head flawlessly, and it is almost possible to immediately forget you are wearing them. They are amazingly comfortable for long periods. Rating 10. The Dylan QS1 weighed 10.5 oz (298 Grams). That is a bit heavier than the Bose, but very nearly as comfortable. Cushy padding on the ear cups and headband, plus a full range of tilt, swivel, and extension adjustments on the ear cups mean these will fit anyone with great comfort. Astonishing, really, for a headphone that costs just $75.00, or 22% of the Bose. Rating 9. The Paww Wavesound 3 weighed in at 12.0 oz (341 grams). The heaviest of the lot, obviously, but the comfort issues do not end there. While the metal headband is appreciated for its probable durability, it is insufficiently padded to equal the other two. It seems okay at first, but a few hours of extended wear had me adjusting these cans on my head periodically. Not horribly uncomfortable, they are just unable to measure up to either of the others. More troubling was the undersized ear cups, which sat on my earlobes instead of fully surrounding my ears (Im an averaged sized guy). Additionally the ear cup padding was not as thick and luxurious as in the Dylans, meaning that the mesh covering the speakers could press against the edges of my ear. I found these comfortable only for an hour or so. Rating 7 On to the Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) feature: The Bose are simply magical. If this is your priority, stop reading right now and buy the Bose. It really isn't even close. Bose ANC is not perfect, but is the best anyone has yet created. Switching on the headphones in Bluetooth mode activates ANC, so it is impossible to use these in BT mode without the ANC active. (The other two allow you to turn the ANC on and off at will in BT mode). That would normally trouble me, but since the Bose is the ONLY one that sounds great with the ANC on, I didn't deduct for this. All of these ANC systems work best on low pitched sounds such as motors, airplane cabin sounds, or the murmur of crowds. The Bose system is astonishing. As if someone turned off the world, muffling and eliminating 80% of the background noise. In my laundry room, they completely block the sound of a clothes dryer (I had to touch it to make sure it was actually running) and greatly muffle the higher pitched sound of the exhaust fan running. I even took them out and ran my powerful leaf blower at full speed with ANC active. While I was certainly able to hear the blower, although at a greatly reduced volume, I did not have to turn the music up to hear every note clearly. Not one notch of extra volume needed. I rate these a 9 because, as I said, nothing is perfect. To rate a 10, they would have to block all sound, something no headphone can do. The Dylan does muffle the sounds, but not nearly as well as the Bose. The instant you switch on ANC without music playing, you hear a generated white noise sound. To be fair, this sound is far less audible once you start the music. But you will be aware of it during every quiet passage. The Bose simply don't do this. Again, the ANC is more effective on low rumbling sound (dryer) than on higher pitches (exhaust fan). The leaf blower while using ANC is louder than with the Bose, but the music is still audible (though not as isolated) with the leaf blower screaming. I didn't need to turn up the volume, and the shriek of the blower drowned out the generated white noise. I rate these a 6. Pretty good. Fantastic if you factor in the price. The ANC on the Paww headset is not impressive at all. It can easily be turned on and off in BT mode. It does muffle deeper rumbling noises, but creates a noticeable and distracting white noise hiss at all times. White noise is especially loud when a higher pitched noise (exhaust fan) is present. You could wear the other two without music playing just to block out the world and let you focus, but the Pawws are pretty much worthless for studying or quiet time. The leaf blower is much more noticeable than with the other two, and requires increasing the volume to clearly hear the music. These are only marginally qualified to be called noise cancelling. I rate them a generous 4. As for appearance and build quality: The Bose are just very unimpressive in this regard. They don't look premium at all, as they are made of basic plastic. My pair is black, because I went to Best Buy and saw the silver display model. Due to all the handling they receive, the color had begun to wear off of both ear cups, giving them a mottled and unattractive look. Im glad I did that, because new the silver look more impressive, and I almost ordered those. The best I can say about the Bose look is that I cant see them when Im using them! As for build quality, they feel quite light and plasticky, prompting me to spend an extra $50 on a two year comprehensive warranty. I rate the appearance a 6, the build quality a 7. The Dylan offer impressive build quality and choice of materials. They look and feel more expensive than the other two, despite being the cheapest. Fantastic! This is one seriously good looking, great feeling headphone. The hundred stars lady was right about that. Dylan should not be able to sell this for such a low price! Every switch and control feels high quality, and the action of the sliding and swiveling ear cups is fantastic. Feels like German engineering. If you tell your friend you paid $200 for these cans, they would have no cause to disbelieve you. These get a rating of 10. The Paww headphones are well crafted, premium looking headphones. Metal instead of plastic in many places adds weight, which is why the comfort suffers. But these are the headphones I feel could survive being thrown off my roof repeatedly. The smaller, less plush ear cups put them a step behind the Dylans. I rate these a 9.5. Finally we come to controls layout and function: The Bose offer you very standard, minimalist controls. Just the on off /pairing slider on the right earcup, and a multifunction button on the edge of that same ear cup. (Play/Pause in the middle, which also can be double clicked to skip ahead or triple clicked to skip backwards. Volume up and down above and below that.) The center button also allows you to answer and end calls, activate Siri, etc. In short, the buttons operate exactly like the ones on your earbud cord. Unimaginative, yes, but there is no learning curve. This rates an 8. The Dylan has a strange arrangements of controls. The small slider switch on the bottom of the right ear cup that goes from Off to BT to BT with ANC is too easy to overshoot, turning off and unpairing when you just meant to just turn off BT. A big triangular button on the right ear cup has a control in each corner. Play pause is in one angle- that works for me. The other two corners are more problematic. One corner you click to skip to the next track, or hold to raise the volume. The other corner is a single click for previous song, or hold to reduce the volume. It is way too easy to skip songs while attempting to adjust volume. Why multifunction buttons? ONE function per button please. Also the volume buttons are backwards- the lower button raises the volume, and vice versa. I rate these only a 6. The Paww headset gets it almost exactly right! The on/off button is in the center of the right ear cup, surrounded by four logically arranged large buttons for Volume Up, Volume Down, Skip Forward, and Skip Back. Perfect! No learning curve at all. The sliding switch on the left ear cup turns the ANC on and off. BUT it is loose, and rattles audibly every time you move your head, which is unacceptable, given that the sound is transmitted directly to your left ear. I could fix it with tape or putty, but why should I be asked to? How can the switch have passed QC? Also, turning the volume up or down results in a beep every notch. Annoying and unnecessary! I rate these controls a ten, with an asterisks for the loose ANC switch (which other reviewers have mentioned, so I don't think its only my set) and the volume adjustment beep. So close to perfect!! So how about sound quality? This is where the rubber meets the road, and in this regard, the three are surprisingly close, especially considering the massive difference in pricing. The Bose have a really great sound, clear and accurate. They effortlessly produce the entire range of sound, from the highest treble to the deepest bass. Fortunately, they suffer none of the booming, overboosted bass so popular in trendy, athlete-endorsed premium headsets. The midrange is clear and unmuddled, even when layered over a strong bass line. Everything is faithfully reproduced, and the effect is just pleasing, balanced sound at any volume level, across all genres. Listening to Holly Coles Train Song, for example, I find that individual instruments are well located and easily discernable. The way the flute stands out even in the midst of the tight thumping bass line is truly extraordinary. And the fact that this all plays out against the backdrop of the eerie silence created by the active noise cancelation is an advantage the others just cannot match. My rating is a 10 (the best you can hope to hear with wireless headphones). The Dylan headphones do a remarkable job reproducing good sound, especially if you consider the amazingly low price. For a tiny fraction of what the Bose cost, you get easily 80% of the sonic purity. Back to back listening will reveal that the bass is boomier and less controlled, the midrange a tiny bit muddy, and the highs not as clear and distinct with the Dylan. Instrumental placement is a bit compromised, as is ultimate dynamic range. Still, if you listen to these without experiencing the Bose, you will likely love them. They do sound better and clearer with the ANC switched off, so whenever possible I think you should go that route. In a noisy environment they will still sound good and do a reasonable job cancelling external noise, and as I stated earlier the ANC generated white noise is tolerable with music playing. I rated these a solid 8. The Paww headphones were the biggest surprise to me. They provide an extremely pleasant listening experience, far beyond my expectations. Several times I found myself just amazed by the accuracy of the notes provided. They sometimes literally made me raise my eyebrows. Being very picky, the bass is a bit looser than what the Bose creates, but again, the price must be considered. For my money (yes I paid for all of these; no one offered me anything for my review) them Paww midrange and treble fully match the Bose. For the current cost of $90, these are a sonic steal. Dynamic range is very well done, and instrumental positioning is amazing. I give these a 9.5, very nearly as good as the $350 Bose offering. IN SUMMARY: The Bose are by far the best of the lot, especially in terms of that amazing noise cancellation. If $350 is not a lot of money for you, buy these and never look back. If that seems like a too much, grab the Dylans and save over $280 on a headset very nearly as good. You will give up almost no comfort, almost no sound quality, and have a more premium looking set of cans. Just be aware that the noise cancellation cannot compare to Bose. The Dylan are a wonderful of headphones, but being the cheapest here makes them an unbelievable bargain. If you can live without world class noise reduction, this is the pair to buy without hesitation! The Pawws are a very good set of BT headphones. They look fantastic, are solid and substantial, and sound just as good as the Bose at $260 less. I would recommend them to anyone who does not need ANC. Just be aware that stronger materials and tougher build do add weight, which becomes noticeable and irritating after several hours of continuous use. Also the noise cancellation is pretty much useless, and the rattling switch that controls it is simply unforgivable. Pawws would be better off losing the noise cancellation and that switch, at least until they can figure out how to do it better. Especially if they could then drop the price. Will any of these headphones give you pristine, studio sound? No. If that is your objective, buy a pair of Sony MDR7506 for $80.00 and learn to live with wired sound. You will then have the world standard for perfect headphone sound. But if Bluetooth and ANC are must haves for you, then you're very likely choosing amongst these three headphones. (I am deliberately ignoring the offerings from Beats, which suffer major sonic flaws (such as lousy, overboosted bass) while costing far more than they are worth. Hope this review helps!

My rating is a 10 (the best you can hope to hear with wireless headphones). The Dylan headphones do a remarkable job reproducing good sound, especially if you consider the amazingly low price. For a tiny fraction of what the Bose cost, you get easily 80% of the sonic purity. Back to back listening will reveal that the bass is boomier and less controlled, the midrange a tiny bit muddy, and the highs not as clear and distinct with the Dylan. Instrumental placement is a bit compromised, as is ultimate dynamic range. Still, if you listen to these without experiencing the Bose, you will likely love them. They do sound better and clearer with the ANC switched off, so whenever possible I think you should go that route. In a noisy environment they will still sound good and do a reasonable job cancelling external noise, and as I stated earlier the ANC generated white noise is tolerable with music playing. I rated these a solid 8. The Paww headphones were the biggest surprise to me. They provide an extremely pleasant listening experience, far beyond my expectations. Several times I found myself just amazed by the accuracy of the notes provided. They sometimes literally made me raise my eyebrows. Being very picky, the bass is a bit looser than what the Bose creates, but again, the price must be considered. For my money (yes I paid for all of these; no one offered me anything for my review) them Paww midrange and treble fully match the Bose. For the current cost of $90, these are a sonic steal. Dynamic range is very well done, and instrumental positioning is amazing. I give these a 9.5, very nearly as good as the $350 Bose offering. IN SUMMARY: The Bose are by far the best of the lot, especially in terms of that amazing noise cancellation. If $350 is not a lot of money for you, buy these and never look back. If that seems like a too much, grab the Dylans and save over $280 on a headset very nearly as good. You will give up almost no comfort, almost no sound quality, and have a more premium looking set of cans. Just be aware that the noise cancellation cannot compare to Bose. The Dylan are a wonderful of headphones, but being the cheapest here makes them an unbelievable bargain. If you can live without world class noise reduction, this is the pair to buy without hesitation! The Pawws are a very good set of BT headphones. They look fantastic, are solid and substantial, and sound just as good as the Bose at $260 less. I would recommend them to anyone who does not need ANC. Just be aware that stronger materials and tougher build do add weight, which becomes noticeable and irritating after several hours of continuous use. Also the noise cancellation is pretty much useless, and the rattling switch that controls it is simply unforgivable. Pawws would be better off losing the noise cancellation and that switch, at least until they can figure out how to do it better. Especially if they could then drop the price. Will any of these headphones give you pristine, studio sound? No. If that is your objective, buy a pair of Sony MDR7506 for $80.00 and learn to live with wired sound. You will then have the world standard for perfect headphone sound. But if Bluetooth and ANC are must haves for you, then you're very likely choosing amongst these three headphones. (I am deliberately ignoring the offerings from Beats, which suffer major sonic flaws (such as lousy, overboosted bass) while costing far more than they are worth. Hope this review helps!

summary: A Beast Of A Receiver
reviewText_clean: Holy cow, this thing is a beast! Prior to finding this Onkyo on Amazon, I had an ill-fated attempt to swap our dead Denon receiver for a new Sony receiver that had received tons of positive reviews. However, the Sony didn't cut it for us, and I went back to the drawing board. Im so glad I found this Onkyo. The RZ810 really is an amazing receiver. First, you should know the RZ line of receivers by Onkyo is their top line for a/v devices. The company also produces a regular line of receivers sold under the NR nomenclature. The RZ810 was near the top of the premium line when it was released, but Onkyo has continued to push the line upward, and now there are several truly high-end models. The RZ810 was a very strong high mid-tier model. You can tell from the box that Onkyo meant for this receiver to be taken seriously. It is big and heavy compared to most other receivers. It dwarfed the Sony I mentioned above. Taking the RZ810 out of the box only enhances the view that this is a premium device. The entire front panel is aluminum, with no plastic to be found. That gives a solid feel even to the door that flips down revealing additional controls and ports. The legs have a premium look to them and were specifically designed for the RZ line. The high-end vibe also carries through to the internals. Onkyo starts with a premium 32-bit/384kHz digital-to-analog converter that faithfully renders music, TV, and movie soundtracks. The RZ810s Dynamic Audio Amplification delivers plenty of power with very little distortion. Due in part to the Phase-matching Bass Enhancement, you will hear and feel a deep rumble when appropriate; our subwoofer has come alive like never before. On top of all that, Onkyo includes a strong 3-year warranty on the RZ line, demonstrating their believe in the quality of what theyve built. Some specs from Onkyo: Power Section Power Output (All channels) 200 W/Ch (6 Ohms, 1 kHz, 0.9% THD, 1 Channel Driven, FTC) 130 W/Ch (8 Ohms, 20 Hz20 kHz, 0.08% THD, 2 Channels Driven, FTC) Dynamic Power 300 W (3 Ohms, Front) 250 W (4 Ohms, Front) 150 W (8 Ohms, Front) THD+N (Total Harmonic Distortion + Noise) 0.08% (20 Hz20 kHz, Half Power) Input Sensitivity and Impedance 200 mV/47 k-ohms (Line)3.5 mV/47 k-ohms (Phono MM) Rated RCA Output Level and Impedance 1.0 V/470 Ohms (Pre Out) 1.0 V/470 Ohms (Subwoofer Pre Out) 200 mV/2.3 k-ohms (Zone Out) 2.0 V/2.3 k-ohms (Zone Pre Out) Phono Overload 70 mV (MM, 1 kHz, 0.5%) Frequency Response 5 Hz100 kHz/+1 dB, -3 dB (Direct/Pure Audio) Tone Control 10 dB, 90 Hz (Bass) 10 dB, 7.5 kHz (Treble) Signal-to-Noise Ratio 106 dB (Line, IHF-A) 80 dB (Phono, IHF-A) Speaker Impedance 6 ohms16 ohms Video Section Video 1.0 Vpp/75 Ohms (Component Y) 0.7 Vpp/75 Ohms (Component PB/CB, PR/CR) 1.0 Vpp/75 Ohms (Composite) Component Video Frequency Response 5 Hz100 MHz/+0 dB, -3 dB Tuner Section Tuning Frequency Range FM 87.5 MHz1070.9 MHz AM 530 kHz1,710 kHz FM/AM Preset Memory 40 stations General Power Supply AC 120 V~, 60 Hz Power Consumption 650 W Standby Power Consumption 0.1 W Dimensions (W x H x D) 17 1/8 x 7 15/16 x 15 9/16 (435 x 201.5 x 395 mm) Weight 30.9 lbs (14.0 kg) If you look at the pictures, you can see you have plenty of connectivity on the back of the receiver. Not only do you have 2 zones, you have 3 zones and a ton of HDMI connections. I should note, only the first three HDMI ports can handle HDR and Dolby Atmos. If you have more than three devices that output those formats, you may want to upgrade to the more recent Onkyo TX-RZ820, but thats virtually the only difference between the two receivers other than about $800 in current prices. The RZ810 connects quickly and easily to WiFi and Bluetooth. The Chromecast function works well, although its not quite as polished as the version found in the Sony. The remote is pretty standard but functional. Note, you can also use the Onkyo Controller App on your smartphone or tablet to control the receiver. Interestingly, many things (such as zone controls) are simply quicker and easier via the app. At the end of the day, the big question for a receiver is how well it processes signals and outputs them. In that regard, this is the best receiver Ive ever used. Sound quality is extraordinary, and not just stuff like the THX Select2 certification for movies that gives you a great directional soundfield. Across the board, music and movies sound clear but rich and full. The bass booms and the subwoofer thumps like never before. The highs are pitch perfect. The mids are clear. The sound is superbly balanced between the speakers to fill the room. Even the video on the television seems brighter and richer. The RZ810 had an original MSRP of $1400, but since it was a 2016 model and the new RZ820 replaced it in 2018, the RZ810 can be found now at roughly a 60% discount, which makes it a terrific value. In case you cant tell, I think the RZ810 a superb a/v receiver. If you need a receiver and can live with only three HDMI ports supporting HDR and Atmos, I highly recommend the Onkyo TX-RZ810.

summary: Arrived "damaged" per Crucial which voided the lifetime warranty.
reviewText_clean: I dislike giving this such a low rating because I hope it's just my bad luck, but this actually was/is my experience. About 6 months agbo I purchased 2 8GB RAM. When I took the sticks out of the packaging the heat spreaders of fins on both of them fell off. I thought this was so odd and I noticed that what holds them on is a 2 sided sticky tape. I didn't think it was much of a problem at the time. But if this happens to you, immediatly send them back and buy different ones or get money back. These worked fine in the first computer build I put them in for about 6 weeks. I then transferred them into a different computer and had some trouble getting them to work correct. It just took several attempts and booting and remounting them and all the tricks necessary to be sure everything is correct. I had no problem them once they were working again. Then I had to change the motherboard and put them in a new motherboard. When I was finished and ready to get the computer started the small test speaker sounded a constant beep beep beep.etc To make a long story short they both eventually were useless in this board and any other mother board I tried them in. I've never heard of Dram/Ram doing this but I thought no problem, lifetime warrenty I'll just get them replaced. I called Amazon first and they said it was too long for them to do anything for me and that I should call Crucial to honor the warranty. I got the RMA and I noticed in the documentation that "any alteration voids warranty". Then I thought oh no, these were the ones that the heat spreaders fell off of. To make matters worse I could only find one out of the four. So I called Crucial and spoke to a person about sending them back without the heat spreaders because they had fallen off. She wasn't sure about this so asked a senior management person and told me the warranty is void because they were damaged. She said I should have immediately sent them back to Amazon. At the time, they cost around $80.00 each. Yeah, I know. So, now I've got a couple of super-duper book markers. What can I do ? Now I'm thinking it was the shipping that caused the "damage" so I shouldn't give one star. I'll give two unless someone can tell me if I'm wrong about rating these so low because of how they arrived. It may have nothing to do with the manufacturing. I doubt that they got too warm too because all my temps were low and I never overclock RAM. I'll raise it to 3. Live and learn. Good luck with yours.

summary: First I ordered these Edifier and was very pleased with the sound quality and bass response
reviewText_clean: I was deciding between these Edifier R1280t, Mackie CR3 and Cerwin Vega XD3. First I ordered these Edifier and was very pleased with the sound quality and bass response. I have them in a 9x9 room sitting on my desk on top of yoga pads about 4 feet apart. Then I thought to order the Cerwin Vega and Mackie to compare them side by side. When I received Cerwin's I plugged them in right away and played some classic rock "Hotel California", very bright sound. I decided to break them in for about 10 hours. Got some improvement, but still they were not close to the Edifiers. Maybe with additional sub they would be better but their sub is over $300, which is ridiculous (You can get SVS sub for $500 which will go down to 20hz easily). Not to mention build quality of the speakers (cheap plastic). Almost forgot to mention how they overheat. Basically I returned them right away. Next I got Mackie. The build quality and feel is very good, sturdy, they look nice and modern. After break in of 20 hours I still could not decide between Mackie and Edifier. Mackie sound very clean and crisp but lack on lows a lot, they would be perfect with subwoofer. After comparing them for 4 days I decided to go with Edifier even though they are not a well known Chinese speaker brand. The build quality is not as good as Mackie, but definitely better than Cerwin. With 2 years of warranty and $100 price tag they will beat any logitech 2.1 system within the same price range. The sound is reach clean and crisp even at high volume. The lows are deep enough for me even when listening to some dance music and not muddy at all. I would recommend these to any one who is looking for a decent pair of PC speakers.

summary: Incredible telephoto for landscape
reviewText_clean: UPDATE: Had an issue with the lens and had to send it in to Tamron for warranty repairs. EXCELLENT customer service experience. The repair was fast. I sent it to them with slow UPS shipping, and had it back in 10 days. Better experience than Nikon customer service. I'm very happy I got this lens! The autofocus with it on my D750 is quiet and fast.... It's so fast that it's hard to tell if it even focused! It's as if nothing happened. It's now my fastest focusing lens. I believe the image quality is actually slightly better than the Nikon/Canon versions. The only reasons to get the more expensive Nikon/Canon version of this lens is if you're a professional who NEEDS your gear to be extremely rugged (i.e., you may get it beaten up), retain its value (for name-brand), and have perfect and top-notch auto focus speed (e.g., sports) because the Tamron may be fast, but is still a bit slower than the Nikon/Canon lenses. Otherwise, the Tamron is just as good if not better in every other category. Some comments: -Happy to get this range for landscapes; I no longer have to haul around primes and a telephoto. Yes, the Tamron is heavy and a bit large, but now I am carrying 2 fewer lenses, and I have a GREAT range for landscape (70-200 is my favorite area to shoot) in 1 lens. -My first weekend shooting landscapes with this (sunrises, mountains, fog, valleys, trees, etc.) and not a single image was bad. All of them were perfectly focused and tack-sharp. The same could not be said for my Sigma 150-500, which constantly missed focus, even at 150mm. -Again, incredible image quality. Tack-sharp. -Focus hasn't let me down yet! -Construction: build seems solid; it is a tad more "plasticky" than the Nikon/Canon, but as long as you aren't abusive, it seems great -Durability: seems durable, but I've not had it for very long. Only time will tell.

summary: First One DOA had Drive Bay Synology 916+
reviewText_clean: As other posters have indicated here, the 916+ hardware seems a little buggy. While the Disk Station I received was both new and unopened, unlike what another poster here experienced (I requested mine be sent in an Amazon box rather than just the OEM packaging, a cautionary step against shipping damage claimed by other purchasers), still mine was a malfunctioning unit right out of the box. Although, it wasn't totally DOA out of the box but in fact, had I not chosen to fully populate the Disk Station with drives, the malfunctioning bay (3) three might have gone unnoticed until much later and left me stuck. So, word of advice is if you buy one of these to check all bays function while it's still under warranty. I'm a lifelong computer scientist and network engineer, so it's not like I'm an amateur at setting up a simple NAS. Nope, no user error here. The brand new Disk Station I got was defective right out of the retail box and it was clearly a hardware defect that should have been caught by Synology's QA if you ask me, assuming they bother to test their units before shipping. After reading some other posts here related specifically to the 916+, I seem to be in good company regarding problematic 916+ hardware. This is not to say Synology's all bad, assuming you get the lucky machine that wasn't manufactured on a Monday that is. Plus, Synology's software and APPs are the basis for most buying decisions with these things and are unquestionably a clinch for the consumer market. My experience so far has been a poor one, since it's a real aggravation to unpack, configure and install one of these things, only to have to reverse everything you did, pack it all up, ship it back and wait for a replacement that's possibly defective as well, again basing this on other posters' experiences found here with the 916+. I will test the next box thoroughly and update this review as appropriate. **** Update 4/30/17 ****** Received replacement and a week after its installation, the disk station is functioning normally. There are pluses and minuses to this model (916+) considering the initial experience related above, but all in all it's a solid solution for middle entry and general purpose. Synology's free apps are a big plus for ease of setup and use. I now recommend the product, realizing I must have just received a lemon. Again, both products were brand new direct from Amazon with no signs of prior sale, damage or tampering, as has been related by others here. Best bet is to buy from Amazon direct since their return policy is insurance against unsuspected trouble....

summary: Battery Supersite -Terrible Battery and Warranty/Customer Service - Avoid this company!
reviewText_clean: I bought this battery and received it on May 23, 2016 to replace a Ritar battery with the same exact specs and amp hours to use with my HillBilly light weight electric golf cart, because in the FIFTH SEASON of using the Ritar battery, it wouldn't go a full 18 holes anymore. The Ritar battery, started slowing down at about the 16th hole so I had to turn off the cart and push it the last 2 or 3 holes. I used this Universal Battery for 5 months until golf season ended here in Colorado November 2016. I Put it on a 2 amp automatic charger after every use and had it on the trickle charger all winter. This Spring, it worked ok the first few times I used it, until it started slowing down around the 16th hole. It's basically performing the same as my 5 year old Ritar battery after only 6 months of use. There was no contact information for Battery Supersite, so I called the manufacturer, Universal Power Group whose rep agreed that the battery should last " at least 3 years used with HillBilly Golf cart only drawing 2 amps. They told me I had to pursue the warranty claim with Battery Supersite and gave me their phone #. I called them 3 times over the course of a week and never got an answer, only a voice message. I left a message each time, but never got a response. I called Amazon, who didn't get an answer from them while I waited on hold. This is the same number that they post on their website for sales. No answer. The Amazon rep emailed BSS with my complaint and I got an email from BSS wanting more information. I emailed them back with the information they requested and I got another email from them telling me about 5 different reasons ( running a golf cart for 18 holes would permantly damage the plates and the battery and other such BS) that would make them not honor the warranty, and that I had to mail the battery back to them, insured, at my expense. I went to the USPS website and entered the dimensions, weight and destination and it totalled $32.63. For a $40 battery that they pretty much told me wouldn't meet their warranty requirements. I emailed them back and told them I didn't want to pay for the return shipping, and that the Golf Cart manufacturer told me the way they handled any battery warranty claims, was to have it tested at an Autozone and email them the results. I also told them that the golf cart manufacturer said that there was plenty of cushion in a 22 amp hour battery for their cart and theirs (Ritar with HillBilly Sticker on top ) usually lasted 3-4 years. My Ritar lasted 4.5 years and still will go as long as the Universal one after 6 months - 16 holes. I asked BSS if there was another way to effect this warranty. I told them I didn't mind sending it back but asked them to send me a pre-paid mailing label which wouldn't cost them as much as it would me. Also I asked them about having it locally tested and to please get back to me and let me know how to proceed. I never received a response, so after 5 days I called Amazon again and Amazon gave me a credit. Amazon is great! Battery Supersite is the worst!

reviewText_clean: It's frustrating that Logitech makes such nice mice... that are so unreliable. Now I'm having software issues with the latest replacement where the mouse connection to my Mac just seems to randomly fail, and the only way to get it working is to un-pair and re-pair it in the unifying software. So as much as I like this mouse, I think I've given Logitech enough chances to fix the problems, but when I have to always have another mouse on hand due to how often this mouse fails it's time to just find a mouse that replaces it completely.

summary: meets my expectations
reviewText_clean: "refurbished" appears to be new. Warranty is shorter. Sound quality is OK. There is no background noise. It can play very loud without much distortion. I set treble to max; doesn't make much difference; maybe it is my hearing but I doubt that. Bass is strong compared to TV sound and to the 2.1 computer speakers I was previously using. Boosting bass results in boomy sound. There is an RCA connector for a separate powered subwoofer. There are 5 inputs: two analog stereo (one via mini/3.5mm phone connector & one via two RCA connectors). One digital via a single RCA connector. One optical. Bluetooth. It is easy to switch between the 5 inputs; the INPUT button on the remote steps through them. However, the indication of which is selected is via an array of lamps; there are no captions. The user must refer to the printed manual. Stepping through the inputs to find one is tedious because there is a delay before the sound is heard. The lamp patterns appear only when the INPUT button has been pressed and that causes the input to change. There is a dedicated button on the remote for Bluetooth. In Bluetooth mode, pressing the INPUT button causes the previously selected input to be selected. Mounting: The are two metric tapings, 22 1/2 inches apart, on the rear. Special screws are provided; these are used with provided brackets. When these are used, the device may be easily placed on & off the wall. That is necessary to access the connectors. The problem is that it is necessary to make four precisely located holes in the wall/mounting surface. A paper template is provided. What I did was to fasten the brackets to a piece of wood, 3 1/2 x 30. I attached my wood to the wall with a single 1/4 lag screw. The wood is completely hidden. The manufacturer should provide a mounting plate with many holes for wall mounting and four holes for the brackets or with the special brackets as part of the mounting plate. There are two non-slip rubber pads on the bottom. They seem ideal for placing the device on a horizontal surface.

summary: Best system on the market but quirky and fragile
reviewText_clean: It's the HTC Vive. It's VR and it's all you can imagine that it would be. The VR experience in this headset is something you really have to experience to understand what the hype is all about. But there are some issues. My number one issue with this device - and why im taking off a star - is because this device can sometimes just be too complicated for typical people. If you're an enthusiast, a PC gamer, and/or someones who has built gaming PCs before, you'll likely keep loving this device like I have but find yourself occasionally frustrated at some of the hoops it will make you jump through to get it working at 100%. When the games are running and everything is already set-up perfectly beforehand, anyone can just jump into a game and play perfectly fine but its all the initial preparation that gets agitating and sets this apart from the simplicity of things like console/2D gaming. Another issue is that the device - for being strapped on to someone to use for actively moving around in VR spaces - is kind of fragile, honestly. You can check the systems subreddit at /r/vive or even some bad reviews on here and you'll find people talking about how the headset isn't waterproof at all and can be made completely unusable by something like sweat from a long session (like an hour) of Space Pirate Trainer or Arizona Sunshine. And then there's issues with the base stations coming out the box with tracking issues and controllers that stop tracking after one good whack against a wall/ceiling fan/TV because the only thing responsible for the controllers tracking is a tiny little wire ribbon. The worst part about this is that some of it isn't covered under HTC's warranty and replacing a single controller or base station can be $130. But I gave this 4 stars - why? Because every fancy new piece of cool tech has it's issues and risks and their developers tend to handle it with -some- grace in most situations. But, if you're willing to take the risks, you've done your homework, and you know how to handle the device, I absolutely recommend it. VR is amazing with the HTC Vive and the tracking is perfect 1:1 when it's set-up the best way. After trying the Oculus, the Vive, GearVR, Cardboard, etc. I think right now HTC Vive is the winning VR hardware. This is the best step in the right direction to the VR I dreamed of as a kid. When these headsets go wireless with 4K-per-eye screens and can affordably track our entire body 1:1 into VR worlds, I'll know I finally saw some really good VR that always seemed like a sci-fi dream. Lastly, my $850 VR set-up would have, uh... just been dropped off at my door and left on my porch had I not been sitting outside waiting for it, so, uh... you might want to watch out for that if you don't live in the best area (I don't - that's why I was waiting). I didn't have to sign or anything. UPDATE: After just short of two months, one of my controller trackpads stopped working - despite me usually babying this thing - so yeah, fragile and prone to hardware failures.

summary: Great All around Laptop!! Gamer or not this thing Rocks!!
reviewText_clean: I did not buy this on Amazon but and eggsellent seller online. :) Quick Summary, This is a great pc with a really fast quad core 6th gen i7 intel processor. The screen is better than a normal LCD panel with wider viewing angles and has very good color and brightness.
