summary: It can do a lot more and for longer ... the 27,000mAh ChargeTech Portable Power Outlet
reviewText_clean: Purpose of Purchasing I play guitar, sing, write my own music and perform (not professionally). There are many event locations where getting AC power is not convenient or the power is unreliable. I think this is great technology that has applications far and wide of the items tested for this review. Full Disclosure: I received a discounted priced unit with the agreement that I would write a review. There were no other stipulations as part of this agreement. My review is my opinion and not swayed by the discount or opinions of ChargeTech. I originally emailed support several times before suggesting the idea of testing and reviewing this product. The communications were and continue to be excellent. For this review, the devices tested exclusively use an external AC->DC Power Supply Unit (PSU) with an AC plug on one end connected to the ChargeTech and the other to an AC->DC converter that plugs into the equipment. Since this covered nearly 95% of every piece of electronic gear I own, it seemed a reasonable approach. Keep in mind that before deciding on what to test, I needed to do the math to determine what I had that could be powered by the PPO AC side. Before receiving the unit, I did a fair amount of research; downloaded specs and the user manual and read-up on the differences between a True Sine Wave (TSW) and a Modified Sine Way (MSW). The AC output of the ChargeTech PPO is a MSW and my initial concerns were that an MSW might cause issues with sensitive electronic gear. Unless the PSU specifically says TSW only AC Input, you have no concerns. All of the gear tested with the ChargeTech PPO for this review, have PSUs supporting MSU AC Power. You should always check for this before plugging it into the PPO or youll likely brick your electronic device and void the PPO warranty. Important Numbers Every modern Power Supply Unit (PSU) comes with the power ratings on the AC Input and DC Output sides the numbers are stenciled or embossed on the PSU. Both the AC and DC information is important to understand first before you plug anything into the ChargeTech PPO. You do not want to void the warranty the ChargeTech offers on their devices. There are a lot of conditions to that warranty so it is recommended that you do your homework first. You need to understand how to calculate the Power Demand on the PPO AC side (the one powering your equipment). There is circuitry on the PPO to warn you about plugging something in with too much power demand, but its not going to prevent you from voiding your warranty or bricking devices. These tests did not challenge the overload circuitry as part of this review. [See Attachment] Pros: The 27,000mAh unit is rated at 500 charges. From zero-to-full takes about 2.5 hours. Thats fast to me in 2016. This will degrade some as the batteries lose efficiency. For this review the unit recharged seven times with no measured difference (to the minute). Sleek design. I like the black unit and it looks great with my pedal system It does what it says it does I can perform on battery with all of my pedals for almost six hours. Con: No replacement battery packs. Once they stop holding a charge, you need to purchase a new unit. Perhaps an altered internal design to support plug and play battery replacement would be more palatable to the wider potential customers who presently DIY DC battery supplies. Conclusion Im enjoying the ChargeTech PPO. It certainly has applications for me beyond music too. I travel so having a great battery for the laptop, tablet, and phone are generally what the PPO was designed for, except in this case - it can do a lot more and for longer. I didn't do a review the USB performance because I cant think of anything new to say about USB Power other than it works, and it works well with this PPO. You can charge a lot of USB devices. summary: Light It Up: A BlueAnt VIVID-BK Black Wireless Mini Bluetooth Speaker Review
reviewText_clean: The BlueAnt VIVID-BK black wireless mini Bluetooth speaker, made in China, measures 3.5 square. Included with the speaker is a USB cable for charging, auxiliary cable, deluxe carabiner style carry clip, and the manual. The top right corner of the speaker has a small rubber loop for use with the carry clip. Control buttons are located on the top and include a play/pause/answer button, volume /skip backward button, volume +/skip forward button buttons, LED themes button, and a mode button. On the side below the rubber loop is a recessed area including the auxiliary port, micro USB port, and power switch which are protected underneath a rubber strip. Like many Bluetooth speakers on the market, this speaker has hands free call capability. Calls are accepted, ended, and rejected using the play/pause button. Pressing the pause/play button twice in rapid succession activates Siri or Google now for voice dialing. Call quality is lacking though. I tried talking to a friend while the speaker sat on the desk in front of me, and he could not understand me. I tried holding the speaker to my mouth and he could hear better, but this was annoying. I just shut off the speaker and used the cell phone. The LED themed lightshow is interesting, but not a feature I would spend money for. Pressing the LED Theme button cycles through the 5 options including lights off. The illumination setting can be altered to control the light activity rate on each option by pressing the LED theme button and the volume down or up at the same time. I have found that when connected, the device needs to be set to full volume for the LED lightshow to work properly. With reduced volume on the device, the LED lights become less active. I can still control the volume on the speaker itself, and if wanted to, can use this likely unintended feature to control the flash rate. The speaker had good sound and gets extremely loud for its size. There is some audible distortion at the highest volume level, but I wouldnt typically use the speaker at full volume. Otherwise, the audio quality is good and pleasing to the ear. As a wireless speaker, the BlueAnt VIVID-BK black wireless mini Bluetooth speaker sounds great and performs well. The lights are interesting, but Id rather save some cash and not have this feature. Additionally, the call quality is just bad. Depending on your desired usage, this speaker may or may not work for you. PROS: 5 Programmable LED themes Built in microphone Siri/Google Now integration 5 hours playtime Splash proof Pleasing sound 1 year limited warranty CONS: Poor call quality

summary: Broken twice in 2 years with gentle use
reviewText_clean: I really do like these headphones. Or I like the concept. For the high cost, I expected to get at least a couple of years out of them. I use the headphones pretty gently. They go in a dedicated compartment on top of my office backpack when not in use and I don't play sports with them or drop them. After a year, I took them out of my backpack one day and the headband snapped in two. First, I couldn't believe they used plastic. Second, I can't imagine what kind of stress could lead it to break. Sennheiser repaired or replaced the headphones under warranty. Less than a year later, I started hearing a rattle in the right earcup, like there was a screw loose. I found the cause: the bluetooth button is broken. I can't remember the last time I used bluetooth, so I don't know how it broke. It still looks fine, but feels dead and won't activate bluetooth. Some part of it has broken off and is rattling around inside. I think the warranty has expired, so it'll be expensive to have Sennheiser repair them. I'd rather put that money toward new (non-Sennheiser) headphones; the headband's probably due to break again soon anyway. Sennheiser doesn't publish any service information (nor do they provide it when asked) and I haven't figured out how to take them apart. It seems this model isn't popular enough for people to make YouTube videos and forum posts about disassembly and service. The only user-serviceable parts are the cushions, the cord, and the battery. IF YOU'RE OKAY WITH FLIMSY HEADPHONES, HERE ARE MY THOUGHTS: When I first got the headphones, I thought they didn't work in amplified mode because the volume was set all the way down. If they seem not to work when turned on, try turning the volume up with the button on the right earcup. They sound quite good to me. The bass isn't emphasized; look elsewhere if you want thumping bass. The bass is better in passive mode with the electronics turned off, though. The noise cancellation does well on rumbles and white noise but doesn't work miracles (it's the reason I bought these and I'm happy with it). The SRS "enhancement' mode sounds terrible to me so I never use it. Sound leakage is minimal; almost zero in passive mode and louder but acceptable when turned on. I returned a pair of Audio Technica ATH-ANC7b because they leaked so much sound that anyone within 10' would get a serenade, even at low volumes. The feature set is great. I love the talkthrough mode; tap the noise cancel button and the 'phones silence the audio and use built-in mics so you can hear everything around you. Great for conversations. I like the way most indicator lights time out and turn off so you're not walking around lit up like a Christmas tree. The detachable cord is a must on any headphones. The removable battery charges via micro USB and can be used while charging if you want another cable hanging off your head. Battery life for corded use with noise cancellation lasts more than a full workday for me, which is all I need. And they fold up pretty compactly for travel. Bluetooth works well. They sync up quickly once paired, all the controls work with my Android phone, and the sound is very good. They work fine with Windows and OSX, too. Range is pretty good; they'll go through a wall or two in my house. I wish I could disable the bluetooth redial feature. A semi-long press on the power button redials the last person you called. That's not something I've ever wanted to do, and I've dialed by mistake more than a few times. The tones you hear for startup/shutdown, noise cancel toggle, bluetooth toggle, and low battery could all be improved. I find them loud and intrusive. On the other hand, it's easy to hear the tones when you're holding the headphones in your hand and pressing buttons. I find them comfortable to wear indefinitely. The cushions are soft and make a good seal to my head. The headband adjusts easily and I don't even feel it on my head. Two stars; all the sound and features in the world don't matter if your headphones are busted.

It seems this model isn't popular enough for people to make YouTube videos and forum posts about disassembly and service. The only user-serviceable parts are the cushions, the cord, and the battery. IF YOU'RE OKAY WITH FLIMSY HEADPHONES, HERE ARE MY THOUGHTS: When I first got the headphones, I thought they didn't work in amplified mode because the volume was set all the way down. If they seem not to work when turned on, try turning the volume up with the button on the right earcup. They sound quite good to me. The bass isn't emphasized; look elsewhere if you want thumping bass. The bass is better in passive mode with the electronics turned off, though. The noise cancellation does well on rumbles and white noise but doesn't work miracles (it's the reason I bought these and I'm happy with it). The SRS "enhancement' mode sounds terrible to me so I never use it. Sound leakage is minimal; almost zero in passive mode and louder but acceptable when turned on. I returned a pair of Audio Technica ATH-ANC7b because they leaked so much sound that anyone within 10' would get a serenade, even at low volumes. The feature set is great. I love the talkthrough mode; tap the noise cancel button and the 'phones silence the audio and use built-in mics so you can hear everything around you. Great for conversations. I like the way most indicator lights time out and turn off so you're not walking around lit up like a Christmas tree. The detachable cord is a must on any headphones. The removable battery charges via micro USB and can be used while charging if you want another cable hanging off your head. Battery life for corded use with noise cancellation lasts more than a full workday for me, which is all I need. And they fold up pretty compactly for travel. Bluetooth works well. They sync up quickly once paired, all the controls work with my Android phone, and the sound is very good. They work fine with Windows and OSX, too. Range is pretty good; they'll go through a wall or two in my house. I wish I could disable the bluetooth redial feature. A semi-long press on the power button redials the last person you called. That's not something I've ever wanted to do, and I've dialed by mistake more than a few times. The tones you hear for startup/shutdown, noise cancel toggle, bluetooth toggle, and low battery could all be improved. I find them loud and intrusive. On the other hand, it's easy to hear the tones when you're holding the headphones in your hand and pressing buttons. I find them comfortable to wear indefinitely. The cushions are soft and make a good seal to my head. The headband adjusts easily and I don't even feel it on my head. Two stars; all the sound and features in the world don't matter if your headphones are busted.

summary: Excellent Mini-ITX Cube Case
reviewText_clean: This really is an excellent case and you can't beat the price. I used this case for a pfSense router build. I wanted something small and I've been on a cube kick, so this is was what I was looking for. Originally, I was going to use the  Core V1 , but I didn't like the lack of dust covers. This case comes with magnetic dust covers that are decent quality. Upon opening my case up, one of the dust cover's magnetic strip wasn't attached to the filter itself. The adhesive probably never fully connected. Pushing it back onto the cover fixed the issue. I really liked the layout of the case. I've never built a mini-ITX machine before but this case offers a nice layout. The power supply area on the bottom has an easily removable dust cover, and the left over space offers more than enough space for hiding cables. The case includes a 3 pin 200mm fan up front. It's massive and maxes out at 800rpm. To me, it was only audible around 650+rpm. Lower than that, I couldn't really hear it. There are two fan mounts in the rear for 80mm fans. It's been a long time since I've used 80mm fans and honestly if you have a good cooler setup, I wouldn't even mount anything in the available space. For my build however, I used an  AMD Athlon 5350  with an  Arctic Alpine M1 Passive Cooling Heatsink . The passive heatsink on it's own was very impressive. However, this machine is going to sit in an area that might need some help with cooling. I added two  Noctua NF-R8  fans, which are incredibly silent for how small they are, and I'd be hard pressed to recommend anything else at that size. My motherboard only had one case fan 4 pin port, and one 3 pin CPU port. I ended up connecting the 200mm front fan to the CPU with a temperature target of 40c and a minimum run speed of 62.5% (it ends up running around 570~rpm). The rear fans are split on the PWM port. Overall, I really like this case and enjoyed building something in it. The design is very pleasing. The construction is solid. It has more space for components that I didn't add, and plenty of space to hide cables. If I was in the market for upgrading my main machine, I'd diffidently consider going mini-itx and using this case. It's just cool. summary: As good as it gets from an iPhone7.
reviewText_clean: If you buy an AudioQuest Dragonfly Red and an Apple Lightning to USB3 Camera Adapter ( which one amazon seller was bundling ) and connect it up to an iPhone7 then connect these headphones to the Dragonfly you'll get state of the art sound. It's simply as good as it gets from an iPhone7. This setup also solves the problem of the iPhone battery dying when you want to keep listening because you can charge the iPhone using the other port in the camera adapter while you're listening, this was important to me. When I played familiar songs using either the apple or amazon music app I couldn't believe how clear and rich the sound was compared to my old cheap headphones or a Bluetooth connection. Of course you pay a price because while this setup is portable it's not exactly convenient because you are connected and the cable on the HE400S is rather stiff plus you've got the camera adapter and Dragonfly. So while the sound quality won't be close to as good if you're going out and about you will be better off with a quality pair of Bluetooth Headphones like the Bose QuietComfort 35 or the V-Moda Crossfade Wireless. A couple of tips on buying stereo stuff, the 1st is you can often buy a product that is open box ( probably a demo ) from an authorized dealer with full warranty at a discount and because in the case of headphones better than new ones because they have been broken in or partially. 2nd it is difficult to determine what to buy, whose reviews do you trust ? I have found over a long time period The Absolute Sound website and magazine have always been correct and the systems I've put together using their "affordable" list have been exactly what I wanted. Finally the sound quality from a setup like this is close to as good as the most expensive high end stereo you could assemble given the same input.

summary: Quality upgrade to cordcutter's network
reviewText_clean: I had sworn off NETGEAR devices after an awful experience with another Nighthawk product, but I'm glad I gave this one a try. It has the looks gamers will love and the performance that anyone seeking to maximize their internet streaming speeds will appreciate. 8-ports deliver on the promise to prioritize and connected devices like a Roku, Apple TV or Amazon Fire TV show marked improvement in terms of glitch-free streaming media. Setup is easy if you follow the directions and if like me you immediately misplace your manual, you can easily find one online in a PDF format. While this could be as easy as plug and play, to get the most out of the device you will need to be somewhat tech-savvy and patient in order to get your network setup just the way you want it. There's a default label on the bottom of the device that has its MAC address, serial number (for registering) and default login info; you will want to change your password from the default "password". You have instructions for accessing the switch info via both a Windows based PC and a Mac. This allows for setting up several different refinements to maximize the switch's performance for gaming and up to 4K streaming media. "The switch comes with three predefined preset modes that let you optimize the performance of the switch with a preset configuration. These modes include a gaming mode, a media streaming mode, and a standard mode." As a cordcutter who depends on streaming media for entertainment along with over air free TV, I use the media streaming mode and it works very well. You can manually setup your own presets too. The default for the device is the standard mode. Managing your Quality of Service (QoS) for individual ports is also available. This thing looks like a mini-spaceship and while the blue lights are cool, they can be shut off too! It's sturdy build-quality and 1 year warranty through NETGEAR make it a good option for upgrading and getting the most out of your gaming and streaming media. NOTE: Your router may override the QoS settings on the switch, so you may have to play a bit with both of them to have them 'play nice'.

As I immediately played back the footage, I noticed there was a significant amount of water inside the case, then the system shut down, to then never work again. She was ready for my response, and was quick to say that their warranty does not cover anything but the case. She said the newer cases come with a water test case for IPADs but that it is "just your misfortune" if you didn't get one. Regardless of what their small print warranty states, their description on Amazon, in bold on their case, and posted on their website states very clearly a guarantee that of false advertisement. If the case isn't fully water-proof then take that advertising off!! If this stops even one customer from buying their products I would feel some form of justice. Thank you for listening to my rant.

reviewText_clean: Took a chance on a refurbished unit and it ended up dying after just barely three weeks of backup use to my regular desktop unit. Maybe it will take one or two returns of bad units to find one that is ok and lasts, but with limited time on a refurbished warranty this might be more of a risk than the price is worth. Probably would be nice to know what exactly they refurbished on each unit when you get it to have an idea what was wrong with it before. If you are ordering this as your only computer, definitely not worth the risk unless you have another laptop or desktop to use if the unit fails.

I can confirm that my laptop fit in the padded compartment without any issues, but the zipper on that pocket began to fail - the half of the zipper that is attached to the bag has is ripping off, which makes it impossible to zip up the bag completely. This began several months ago (probably around the 10 month mark) and has gotten progressively worse with time. I used the bag for carrying the laptop, some folders, and occasionally clothing for short trips, so the day-to-day use has not been strenuous, and it's extremely disappointing to see that the touted Swiss Gear is of such unremarkable quality. The bag is absolutely not worth paying more than $50 to $70, but even in that range I would suggest finding an alternative that can hold up better. If you don't mind buying a new backpack in a year and you like the brand, then by all means buy it; but it won't reliably last longer than that. Unfortunately it has reached the point where it is no longer realistically usable - I will be contacting Swiss Gear to see how the warranty holds up, and may revise the score upwards if their support is good.

reviewText_clean: Update 1/14/17 - This is by far the worst motherboard I've ever owned. The hardware, itself, is unreliable and glitchy. -Couple that with Asus' software and you have a recipe for disaster! Over the last 24-hour period, I think the system has crashed over two-dozen times. -This is with a fresh Win10 install, manufacturer spec approved components (ram, video, proc) and running stock settings (no overclocking- my god... that'd be insane as it's not even stable at base freq!). -Opening any application results in a complete system failure (not even a bsod) where the system completely locks up and only if I'm lucky reboots, normally I have to perform a hard shut-down and start again. -No dump files, no errors in sys log, nothing. -This being my second board of this model, I'm starting to believe the "in search of incredible" slogan at startup, however, I would posit that Asus has yet to being their search as the only thing incredible about this steaming pile of excrement is how horrible it is. The first board I received had a bad memory channel. (after buying, I became painfully aware that this is a common defect for this particular model) After reading the acceptable memory guide to the ASUS technician and insisting that my Corsair Dominator Platinum memory was indeed on the list, they offered to RMA the board. -I wasn't satisfied with their timeline / cost to ship my board to them to warranty their product, but thankfully Amazon's return process is excellent. My new board arrived and thus I'll begin my review: The board is big in every way... make sure your case is roomy. Their firmware update is easy-enough but a lot of the advertised features don't work exactly as advertised. -The online update has never worked, no matter how I hold my tongue or what ports I open on my firewall. My main pain point has to do with their "Power Saving" power plan. My I7-5820k will actually get stuck at 799Mhz and requires a reboot to get it out of that mode. As long as the system doesn't go to power save and straight to hibernate, I'm fine. Several calls to ASUS hasn't produced a fix for this issue.

summary: Worked great but cannot rebuild and array
reviewText_clean: This was my second NAS. Before I had an ASUS that proved unreliable over time and I did not want to take any more risks with my data so I shelled out the cash for this bad boy as it seemed reliable. It was awesome for 4 years but then one of the drives failed. Initially I was calm about it, but getting it back up was a bigger and bigger head ache. This device in my opinion is not future proof. Its barely proof at all. The first issue is the list of hard drives that work with it is I believe 5. And that's not 5 "types", that's 5 product specific drives down to the exact 10 digit product model. WD no longer makes them and even places that claim to carry them and charge double or triple the cost of a similar drive actually cannot ship you what you asked for, and there lies the problem. The DX4000 will not work with any drive unless it matched the exact product code it has pre-loaded into it on a "white list". So I got in touch with WD and they kindly sent me a new one as I was just within warranty. However the first one they sent was not a match. So I sent it back. I then had to wait for them to receive it back, check it, and then ship a replacement. When it arrived I loaded it into the machine and it appeared to work. However it never ran the same. Now after 2 years on and off I have given up, I don't believe it ever rebuilt the raid array as it was designed to do. It now has a ton of errors and failed software start ups and I have lost a third of the capacity so i am down to 8TB of 12TB(16TB). The LCD doesn't read any more other than to say "Loading OS please wait" and I cannot seem to work out how to fix it even through I have read lots of knowledge groups etc. Bummer, It proved no more reliable and well made as the ASUS on I had before. onto Synology, hopefully their designs are better. Certainly the limited HD list on the WD was ridiculous.

reviewText_clean: Worked well until a few weeks ago. When we went to start it up, it only showed a plain white screen. Tried resetting (with the refresh+power buttons) to no avail. Tried reinstalling Chrome from a recovery USB drive (and then a recovery SD Card), but after the recovery process completes, every single time it goes back to the "Chrome is missing or corrupt" screen. I tried this full recovery many times, using different brands of USB and SD cards for the recovery medium (as I read some brands don't work as well as others). Researching the problem further on google's chromebook support forums, it appears this means the 16GB Flash Memory (the SSD) has failed. The memory is integral to the motherboard, so there is no way to replace just the "hard drive" as you could in a traditional laptop. I asked Asus support if there was anyway to run Chrome off an external memory card (SD Card) and they basically said they "can't support modifications to the unit". So, 6 months out of warranty, $200 of plastic and lead into a landfill it shall be.

summary: Some good and bad, but mostly the ugly - Potentially the slowest buggiest Android 6.0 tablet ever.
reviewText_clean: Potentially the slowest buggiest Android 6.0 tablet ever. OK, so for the price I had low expectations for multi-tasking etc. Still, even with those low expectations I am let down by this tablet. It's not that it doesn't work, but it's slower than my 3 year old Samsung Galaxy Tab on KitKat that I wanted to replace after dropping it and smashing the screen. The apps take a LONG time to open, and then when you want to go back and view the home screen it takes a good 20 seconds before the apps on the screen show up. Don't try using the tablet while it's charging via mini-usb either. If you do, the screen has a mind of its own. Typing words creates a bunch of spaced gibberish and backspace or highlighting won't delete. It charges, but that's about it. Possibly the reason it comes with an old fashioned charger. Even now as I type this on the tablet itself the volume display keeps opening and closing even though I'm nowhere near the volume buttons on the keyboard or the display and I'm not even charging it. It's a buggy/defective UI. Typing this with the awesome (but small) keyboard and the cursor keeps jumping up to lines I typed above. I love the keyboard and magnetic attachment to the tablet. I love that the tablet goes into a 'desktop mode' when attached and that there's a 'mouse' like part on the keyboard. For $109 the display is adequate without being bright, but it's good enough I suppose. Battery life - I really can't comment. It came fully charged and drained by the end of setup and downloading from backups. I've recharged it, but so buggy I don't think I'll give it a chance to discharge again. I've had a lot of android devices and none have ever behaved so poorly... especially a newer one (2016 model?!?!). I'm happy I purchased from Amazon as I'll be returning the product and the extra warranty I purchased. I'll spend the extra few $ and get something of a better brand/quality. Seems they put more thought into the keyboard than the tablet. Few other things to note - the entire thing is plastic. The tablet is light.. it's nice that it has premiums that Ihave never seen on other tablets like all the ports for HDMI, USB, SD Card etc and ability to connect a mouse. Also like that you can choose SD as your default storage space. Still - just can't deal with the buggy OS. Bluetooth is another problem. Fine for music, but for video the lag between the picture and when the audio actually gets to your ears is about 1-2 seconds delayed. Worse than watching an overdubbed karate movie by far. I use the same bluetooth headphones with other tabs/phones and pc and don't have a noticeable delay, so it's definitely the tab. I've had a lot of android devices and none have ever behaved so poorly... especially a newer one (2016 model?!?!). I'm happy I purchased from Amazon as I'll be returning the product and the extra warranty I purchased. I'll spend the extra few $ and get something of a better brand/quality. The tablet is light.. it's nice that it has premiums that Ihave never seen on other tablets like all the ports for HDMI, USB, SD Card etc and ability to connect a mouse. Fine for music, but for video the lag between the picture and when the audio actually gets to your ears is about 1-2 seconds delayed. Worse than watching an overdubbed karate movie by far. Nearly identical in features and with the Manfrotto name. There is an amazing difference in the feel of these two tripods. The Manfrotto legs feel secure and stay in position, wheareas the Vanguard/Alta feels weak and insecure. The Manfrotto costs about $50 more and is well worth it. I really wanted to like this tripod, it is such a great concept. Unfortunately, the implementation and execution of the design is sub-par. If you use your tripod regularly, you will probably be disappointed if you buy this item.

summary: Fuji Does Not Honor their Warranty
reviewText_clean: I purchased this camera about 10 months ago. About 5 months ago, it started having a problem where it would not power on despite having a full battery unless I removed and reinserted the battery. I sent it in to Fuji repair and they sent it back several weeks later with no information at all on what repairs, if any, had been done. The only evidence that they had done anything was that the camera had been reset to factory default settings. It continued to have this problem so I sent it back again--this time checking the box indicating my willingness to accept a refurbished replacement. They sent it back with the hastily scrawled words "factory specs" and an indication that the "repair" person had turned it on and off 50 times and it worked every time. That's surely true, because it has this problem only sporadically, maybe once every few days of use. Within a few days I saw that it was having the same problem, and now when I turn it on sometimes that back screen flashes on and off about 10 times before going black. Now sometimes the camera reads F0 (an impossible aperture), even with a lens solidly attached (again, taking out the battery and reinserting it fixes the problem, but this is not acceptable especially given that the battery compartment placement requires removal from a tripod before accessing the battery compartment). I don't understand the logic of Fuji here. If I am willing to accept a completely random, possibly dysfunctional refurbished replacement, why would I lie about my camera having a problem? Or are they saying that I am too stupid (or possibly hallucinating) to know if there is a charged battery in the camera? Anyway, I have purchased a couple thousand dollars in lenses and was going to buy the X-T2 as well, but certainly that won't be happening if they don't honor their warranty commitments.

Granted, this computer is in a totally different price bracket so that's completely understandable. However, I feel like sometimes it's overly bright and kind of washed out. BUT, it is by no means bad. It's still decent, just not the best. - Screen feels somewhat flimsy to the touch because of the plastic casing. I'd say it's totally typical of a windows laptop. One of the reasons I opted for this machine instead of a similarly-priced ASUS ROG machine was because a lot of the reviews noted that the ASUS ROG machine has a VERY flimsy screen. Since the screen is one of the only parts of the machine you can't really replace yourself that easily, I opted for this MSI instead. - Keyboard is one of those ridiculous ones that has the number pad included on the right hand side so the keyboard is not centered on the machine. I CANNOT STAND this feature and it's almost impossible to find a Windows laptop nowadays that doesn't do this. It also prevents the mousepad from being centered - another annoyance. I wish manufacturers offered a centered keyboard option. - Mousepad sometimes picks up inputs when the edge of your thumbs swipe across it mistakenly while typing. It's also a very basic mousepad with physical buttons (which I actually like), but it doesn't respond well to gestures of any type. - Comes with Norton Antivirus. WHY??!! I removed it right out of the box. - Windows is set up to automatically save everything to the smaller SSD instead of the larger HDD, so you'll have to reconfigure this right out of the box. - All plastic casing - no metal. It gets smudgy quite easily. - Speakers are located on the front of the laptop around the frame, which, if you're not sitting at a desk, get covered up easily and inhibit sound. The sound quality isn't that bad, but the placement of the speakers really inhibits the sound for the user. I prefer the location of speakers to but under the screen above the keyboard since that way there's no interference from objects or people blocking sound. CONCLUSION Overall, I'm very happy with this machine so far. I've had it for a few weeks and have not had any problems with it yet. I plan on updating this review in a year if nothing else comes up with it. At this point, I'd recommend this laptop. Blessings!

This is still not very good for you the buyer since you can't determine before hand if it's going to work for you. Read the full review before buying: Full Review: Ok ... I'm pretty sure I read the description of this adapter completely when I bought it ... but re-reading it ... the 2nd to last bullet states that it's not compatible with "low power HDMI ports such as the MacBook Pro with Retina Display". Hmmm wonder if it's been updated in the last week ... Well I can confirm that that is the case and I had to return it for exactly that reason. What happens when plugged into my MacBook Pro is that the Mac recognizes a device is plugged in and switches the display to HDMI and then thinks that the HDMI device was removed switches back ... and then it repeats. From a customer perspective ... Really ... lets put the burden on the user to know if they have a HDMI port which can supply enough current to run Moread's adapter? Oh yes but they listed that MacBook Pro specifically as incompatible ... buried on the 4th bullet ... between a statement that reads like they are compatible with all HDMI ports ("Compatible with PC, laptop, notebook, Apple TV, Roku streaming media player, cable box, and other devices with HDMI port") and "Limited 1-year warranty" ... So how should I rate this device? Lets see ... who is responsible to make sure that the adapter is compatible with the devices HDMI port? A) the user? Short of knowing what your HDMI port can supply and knowing what Moreads adapter draws we can't do it. B) the manufacture of the device with the HDMI port? Does it meet the minimum HDMI spec? If it does they are not to blame. C) Moread engineering to design to the minimum HDMI spec. Hmmm ... this is what engineers are suppose to do ... Are there other devices out there that are engineered to this minimum spec and work ... YES definitely. Hmmm ... guess Moread gets a star maybe two but no more for a poorly engineered device and a marketing group who feels that they can push that poor engineering off on the user ... Even if it does work with someone who has the same PC as you do ... it might not work with yours as HDMI ports are designed to guarantee a minimum spec. The actual current a port can supply varies from unit to unit and over temperature but will always meet that minimum ... so even if it works one day I'd not depend on it working the next. I can not recommend this device ...

summary: Bang For Buck, A Best Value!
reviewText_clean: After being a Canon shooter for years and having a substantial investment in EF-mount glass, I was in the market for a compact system I could take abroad that would provide the high-quality stills I was accustomed to capturing with the larger DSR's. Through much investigation, I ended up with this body about a year ago and I think I'm in a place to throw down a few thoughts on it now. This will be far from a detailed review as I don't use many of this camera's functions - just sticking with what I know... I mostly use this body with EF (Canon/Zeiss), FD, (really old Canon), and M (Leica) mounted lenses. I had a chance to borrow two native mount lenses for a month, Loxia 35mm & 50mm, thank you Zeiss! I have a flick-site with dedicated albums of photos taken with various lenses attached to the Sony - please search for "Fret Spider" and click on the albums tab for each type of lens. With the Canon EF Metabones IV adaptor, auto-focus was inconsistent, particularly in darker environs. But this didn't really bother me, I mostly use manual lenses on the Canon bodies with LiveView and magnification - I was able to port over the same methodology on the Sony. Therefore my migration to this system was perhaps easier than those that rely on automatic focus systems. The focus-peaking feature is very useful, but it doesn't always guarantee dead-on focus with super-wide aperture lenses - I found that magnification is really the only way to be certain. For Canon's FD lenses, this camera is a beautiful thing, truly breaths new life into that (sometimes radioactive!) glass. For Leica M lenses, it's a bit more complex and this might burst the bubble of some; the combination will not avail the full potential of the sensor or lens. My experience echoes what I've read with regard to how the light exits the rear of the Leica (or M-mount) lens and its angle of incidence with the Sony sensor stack. In the middle of the frame, there's no problem but as you get to the edges things don't fare so well for wide-angle lenses - decreased resolution & contrast and increased shading & color smearing become more prevalent as the focal length gets shorter starting with around 50mm. The Zeiss Loxia 50mm and adapted Otus 55mm have sharper extreme corners than the APO 50mm Summicron (yes, that Leica lens) - this is with all lenses being stopped down to around f/8 - f/11. In saying that, the 50mm Summicron with the Voigtlander Close-Focus adaptor is probably my favorite lens to attach to this body, crazy small package with deceptively amazing results wide open and very good stopped down! For their cost however, lenses in the Zeiss Loxia series give fantastic results, particularly when stopped down, if you like manual lenses. The stabilization system works ok given that nearly all my usage was with non-native lenses - the native mount lenses may do better. With Leica lenses, I don't feel there's much assistance and I end up turning off the stabilizer - possibly given their petite size, maybe it doesn't adjust correctly ? For the Canon EF or FD mount lenses, I've witnessed more assistance. The menus are not as difficult to navigate as others may have eluded to, once you figure out where things are, the navigation becomes second nature. If I had used Sony for years and suddenly switched to Canon, I would probably be in the same boat The whole compressed 14-bit thing is a bit overblown. With over 40k exposures on this camera, I have yet to find artifacts of the compressed raw files people talk about - I pixel peep and my lenses aren't a limiting factor. The battery life (as everyone else mentions) blows and I find that manually turning off the camera between scenes of interest is really the best way to conserve the battery and last an entire day of say, site-seeing. I just keep wondering when I'm going to wear out that switch and render the camera useless! Compared to the new A7R II (which I have recently acquired)... unless you're going to be blowing your photos up to poster-sized dimensions (more than a meter on any side) and allowing your audience to really get close to the print, there's not much perceptive difference between the two cameras from a stills perspective - so buy this camera instead, save your money and buy a better lens. Picture quality is exceptional on this camera. As a Canon user, the extended dynamic range on this body and the newer A7R II is quite impressive as everyone raves - yes, you can theoretically pull out details from deep shadows, but if you get your exposure correct, you really shouldn't have to pull up your shadows by 5 stops. I like taking pictures of cityscapes at night, and this thing delivers on long (30 second) exposures. However, for true nasty weather (rain & blizzards) conditions, I still grab my Canon 5D3 - I just don't have the confidence in the A7II that it will take the beating. I can't speak much for the video and auto-focus capabilities of this camera, so you'll need to read other reviews to get more info on those features. My only thought is that if you're interested in an inconspicuously small (albeit solid) camera body that is packed with features and possessing exceptional picture quality, I highly recommend at least renting the A7II and seeing for yourself, if this style of camera suits your needs. Peace and happy shooting!

After being a Canon shooter for years and having a substantial investment in EF-mount glass, I was in the market for a compact system I could take abroad that would provide the high-quality stills I was accustomed to capturing with the larger DSR's. Through much investigation, I ended up with this body about a year ago and I think I'm in a place to throw down a few thoughts on it now. This will be far from a detailed review as I don't use many of this camera's functions - just sticking with what I know... I mostly use this body with EF (Canon/Zeiss), FD, (really old Canon), and M (Leica) mounted lenses. I had a chance to borrow two native mount lenses for a month, Loxia 35mm & 50mm, thank you Zeiss! I have a flick-site with dedicated albums of photos taken with various lenses attached to the Sony - please search for "Fret Spider" and click on the albums tab for each type of lens. With the Canon EF Metabones IV adaptor, auto-focus was inconsistent, particularly in darker environs. But this didn't really bother me, I mostly use manual lenses on the Canon bodies with LiveView and magnification - I was able to port over the same methodology on the Sony. Therefore my migration to this system was perhaps easier than those that rely on automatic focus systems. The focus-peaking feature is very useful, but it doesn't always guarantee dead-on focus with super-wide aperture lenses - I found that magnification is really the only way to be certain. For Canon's FD lenses, this camera is a beautiful thing, truly breaths new life into that (sometimes radioactive!) glass. For Leica M lenses, it's a bit more complex and this might burst the bubble of some; the combination will not avail the full potential of the sensor or lens. My experience echoes what I've read with regard to how the light exits the rear of the Leica (or M-mount) lens and its angle of incidence with the Sony sensor stack. In the middle of the frame, there's no problem but as you get to the edges things don't fare so well for wide-angle lenses - decreased resolution & contrast and increased shading & color smearing become more prevalent as the focal length gets shorter starting with around 50mm. The Zeiss Loxia 50mm and adapted Otus 55mm have sharper extreme corners than the APO 50mm Summicron (yes, that Leica lens) - this is with all lenses being stopped down to around f/8 - f/11. In saying that, the 50mm Summicron with the Voigtlander Close-Focus adaptor is probably my favorite lens to attach to this body, crazy small package with deceptively amazing results wide open and very good stopped down! For their cost however, lenses in the Zeiss Loxia series give fantastic results, particularly when stopped down, if you like manual lenses. The stabilization system works ok given that nearly all my usage was with non-native lenses - the native mount lenses may do better. With Leica lenses, I don't feel there's much assistance and I end up turning off the stabilizer - possibly given their petite size, maybe it doesn't adjust correctly ? For the Canon EF or FD mount lenses, I've witnessed more assistance. The menus are not as difficult to navigate as others may have eluded to, once you figure out where things are, the navigation becomes second nature. If I had used Sony for years and suddenly switched to Canon, I would probably be in the same boat The whole compressed 14-bit thing is a bit overblown. With over 40k exposures on this camera, I have yet to find artifacts of the compressed raw files people talk about - I pixel peep and my lenses aren't a limiting factor. The battery life (as everyone else mentions) blows and I find that manually turning off the camera between scenes of interest is really the best way to conserve the battery and last an entire day of say, site-seeing. I just keep wondering when I'm going to wear out that switch and render the camera useless! Compared to the new A7R II (which I have recently acquired)... unless you're going to be blowing your photos up to poster-sized dimensions (more than a meter on any side) and allowing your audience to really get close to the print, there's not much perceptive difference between the two cameras from a stills perspective - so buy this camera instead, save your money and buy a better lens. Picture quality is exceptional on this camera. As a Canon user, the extended dynamic range on this body and the newer A7R II is quite impressive as everyone raves - yes, you can theoretically pull out details from deep shadows, but if you get your exposure correct, you really shouldn't have to pull up your shadows by 5 stops. I like taking pictures of cityscapes at night, and this thing delivers on long (30 second) exposures. However, for true nasty weather (rain & blizzards) conditions, I still grab my Canon 5D3 - I just don't have the confidence in the A7II that it will take the beating. I can't speak much for the video and auto-focus capabilities of this camera, so you'll need to read other reviews to get more info on those features. My only thought is that if you're interested in an inconspicuously small (albeit solid) camera body that is packed with features and possessing exceptional picture quality, I highly recommend at least renting the A7II and seeing for yourself, if this style of camera suits your needs. Peace and happy shooting!

reviewText_clean: Received as a Christmas gift (my friend did buy it on Amazon) and finally set it up 3/18/17 after the Pyle unit developed a line down the screen. I'm disappointed big time with it. First, it appears to be nothing more than a rebranded Pyle unit (presuming Pyle is even a "real" brand) and it's even worse than the Pyle was. The thing is mechanically noisy when the motor is running; my cars are more quiet at idle. Image quality is mediocre; ditto audio. Sometimes the screen goes black for a couple of seconds, other times the image breaks up and is "pixelated". On playback the image also freezes up at times or skips ahead. Sometimes when starting a DVD I can hear it run for a few seconds as if it's scanning the disk, then it stops and does nothing. All these problems are worse with dual layer DVDs. Audio isn't in sync with the video. As with the Pyle player the screen ratio setting control does nothing; it's stuck on wide sceen. The positive reviews and screen size led me to ask for it as a Christmas gift. Comparing my experiences with this to those reviews all I can conclude is manufacturing quality control must be nonexistant. There was a card packed with the unit inviting you to contact the maker if you weren't happy. Did that detailling all the problems; there was no response. Over the years I've had several players like this (Polariod, Phillips, Pyle, etc) and this is the worst of them. I really wanted to like this thing but it's junk.

reviewText_clean: BE AWARE, THIS IS A 10/100 POE INJECTOR ONLY -- NO GIGABIT. You should also make sure your device adheres to the 802.3af PoE standard, as non-standard devices might fry (see the poor SOB who left the 1-star review) and 802.3at devices won't get enough power. Bought this to use with my  TP-Link EAP245 access points  and it does what it says on the box, providing power to the access points. It's a good value, cheaper than many other multi-device PoE solutions, but has a few shortcomings that keep it from getting five stars. First, there's no documentation to speak of other than a label on the underside with mixed Chinese/English, though enough is in English that you can figure out what's going on and hopefully get it hooked up right (though another reviewer noted that the label was on backwards on his unit, so YMMV). Second, there are no "keyholes" in the bottom to wall-mount the box; the little round holes with the slits so you can put them on a set of screws and slide them into place. A little device like this just begs to be wall-mounted, but it's not happening here unless you're ready to crack open the case and void your warranty/return. Third, there's no labeling on the sides or top. A subtle raised or embossed "DATA" and "POE" legend either on the faces with the ports or the top along the appropriate edges would've been great. It'd eliminate the possibility of a label getting applied incorrectly, and allow you to see what goes where without having to flip the box over to look.

summary: Alot of Features, Really Nice Unit
reviewText_clean: I spent alot of time researching before I ordered this unit. Key features I wanted were: *Dashcam and GPS in one *Easy mounting *Driver safety alerts (land wandering, too close to car in front, etc.) *Ability to respond to voice commands *Bluetooth feature allowing for connection to my smartphone to do hands-free calls and have text messages read to me *Ability to tie into live traffic feeds without paying additional subscription charges This Garmin has everything on my list. Voice commands have worked well so far; it pins down the list of related addresses, you select one and you're on your way. I had tried to also type some addresses it and found it to be a bit awkward in what it located. For example, I typed in my street address and it decided to search for results in Pennsylvania. I live in Illinois. I could have gone the step of typing in city/state after giving the street address, but wanted to see how on the mark it was without doing so. You can also use it to search by category so if you need to quickly find a gas station nearby, that can be done promptly. Directions have been accurate so far. Really enjoying this unit and its features. I bought one that was refurbished by Garmin, it comes with a one-year warranty, so I was very comfortable going with a used unit to help get the price down.

summary: Held Together With Hopes and Dreams...and Little Else
reviewText_clean: "Ya hear me, baby? Hold together!" - Han Solo, talking to the Millennium Falcon So, people aren't kidding when they say that this thing is really cheaply made. I've had this thing in my possession for about an hour, now, and the sliding mechanism is already getting loose. The "locks" to keep it in place at either end seem to be working, though I have my doubts about their long-term durability, but there's no lock to keep it in place in the middle. Either connector is going to end up poking out. Plus, with the (very) cheap plastic that this thing is made of, I don't think I'm going to be able to keep it on my keychain, like I intended to, for fear of it breaking apart and falling off. I mean, perhaps if I encased it in a shell of superglue, it might hold together...but I'd really like to avoid doing that. As for the functionality, I can't comment too much on that just yet. (Warning: Techie details ahead) It has worked with every machine that I've plugged it into; Mac OS 10.10, Mac OS 10.11, Windows 10, and Ubuntu Linux 15.10, and it's been formatted to exfat. My Motorola Nexus 6 running Android 6.0.1 wanted to reformat it before use, but I downloaded a plugin for my file browser of choice, SolidExplorer, and it worked beautifully. "I've made a lot of special modifications, myself." - H. Solo. It seems like this drive will continue to serve me well from a data storage standpoint. The device seems to work, but really, the manufacturing seems like it would be a bit of an embarrassment point for SanDisk. If it ever breaks, I really hope that they're willing to replace it, or give me my money back. I paid about $18 for it during an Amazon Gold Box deal...let's hope it's worth even that over the long-term. The packaging says that it comes with a 5-year warranty. Hopefully, I won't have to test that. TL;DR: Much like the beloved Falcon in Empire Strikes Back, if this thing holds together, it should serve me well.

summary: Beware No Warranty
reviewText_clean: Beware. Panasonic does not honor their 1 year warranty. I called their customer service. They claim this was an import not a US branded model and that violates the warranty. They said that you cannot tell from the model number or serial number on the camera whether it is or isn't covered by warranty, when bought from Amazon. When you register the unit they do not tell you whether it is covered or not. The registration site refers you to Square Trade for three year extended warranty - where they mention having defect related and accident related damage and foreign purchase coverage - but they don't say just what is covered but only imply it does. When you get the confirmation read it because the fine print says it does not cover ADH Accidental damage from handling. This was not mentioned by Square Trade until you call to try to buy it. If you call Square Trade about it they say it cost an additional $75 for 3 years coverage (one more year than what Panasonic won't honor) but they won't even sell it to you and refer you back to Panasonic. This seems like very deceptive trade practice certainly with Panasonic, maybe also with Square Trade. Canon and Sony are more honorable companies. About the DMC-SZ50. It is a very nice camera but the lens shutter jams both open and shut but works otherwise. It wasn't damaged - it just failed. No way to prove that. Would Square Trade call it a defect and repair it, or would they call it ADH and not? I don't know. My first Lumix DMC ZS3 (2009) lasted 4 years before it developed a lens shutter problem. This one about 6 months. Weakest link in an otherwise fine camera. I wish they just removed the shutter and replaced it with a lens cap.

reviewText_clean: I actually purchased two of these in May 2016 two years ago today's date. However they sat on a shelf until today. Of course I am way beyond any kind of warranty period whatsoever. My wife and I decided to finally try these out today. The first package we opened was obviously a returned item and was missing the instructions and all the parts were loosely scattered. However, the instructions included ilwith this item are a joke. A small pamphlet showing icons that presume items will fit one another. Both items do not work at all. summary: Works great with Raspberry Pi (all models)
reviewText_clean: This display can be easily modified to work with a Rapsberry Pi and operate at 5 volts. Remove the DC buck converter IC and move the V+ lead (red wire) to the IC pad for output (pin 2). Cut the other end of the power lead and connect to ground and 5V on the GPIO header to power the display from the Pi. This will void any warranty of course and I do not recommend this for beginners. Parts are very delicate inside the display. The Data sheet for the buck converter can be found online. With the sellers permission I can post a link to that. This is a fantastic alternative to more expensive TFT hats that hog the GPIO header. Im building a handheld emulator and this fits the bill nicely. Thank you. Will purchase again for future products.

reviewText_clean: I bought this glass in April 2015 because I have decided to switch over to all Sony glass after purchasing three Sony alpha cameras. I mainly use this for portraits and the results were great. When working with this the picture quality was stunning. I sent the lens in for repair as it was still under warranty and that process was quiet easy. Unfortunately, when returned, I had a note from the repair center that the lens had been tampered with and that they would not open it for repair. This was obviously quite disconcerting given that it was bought from Amazon and assumed new (which I believe it was) and the cost of $1600. I will continue my discussion with them to see if it can be resolved and will update as appropriate, but given the cost of this lens, I felt a review of warning was in order for other buyers. 1/26 So I said i would update if I had new info...unfortunately Sony refused to budge on the word of their repair place who refused to give any kind of indication of how it was tampered with. So although I can not necessarily recommend this lens, I can say that if you buy it on Amazon, they back their products in a reasonable and fair way. Perhaps I just got a lemon, but I will continue to purchase lens from Amazon.

I had to disable the under/over current sensor to make use of it. The second was one I bought personally, this one was completely dead (did not work as a battery backup) after only 3 years (or, at least that's when I finally noticed it was dead after a few years of very few power outages). I called to get support, and was told that the warranty was a 3 year warranty. I bought that unit 3 years 6 months prior, so I was not covered. The support agent told me that the unit was older (around 6 years). I told him I have no idea when it was made, only when I actually bought it. I asked if there was a date stamped on the package or some way to know for next time, and he politely accused me of buying the unit 6 years ago... I didn't really know what to say. Meanwhile, the power is out right now and my TEN year old, cheap ($50) APC power backup in the other room is still purring away. It looks like I'll buy APC next time.

reviewText_clean: This was a pretty good router for the first 6-12 months or so. The range was good and the Net Genie app is very useful if you have kids and like remote control. But the problems started about 4 months ago for me. As not to get into a lot of details, I'll just name a few main problems I had. 1. Ethernet Port #3 would intermittently go in and out. This lasted for about 2 months and finally it just quit working all together. 2. Ethernet speeds could be erratic at times. I had a lot of problems with all 4 E. Ports defaulting to 10Mb/s. I have 100Mb/s Cable. Once the #3 Ethernet port quit working completely the other 3 ports started to maintain 100Mb/s. 3. Port Forwarding settings will sometimes reset back to default. 4. Renaming the DHCP Clients in the Net Genie app would sometimes reset and I would have to get everyone's IP again to know who was who. When I bought this router it was a little pricey for me. So, on that note, I don't think I could recommend it to anyone unless it was 50% or more off. Its more of a hand-me-down router than anything. You shouldn't have to replace your router every year.

summary: Excellent body construction, good performance.
reviewText_clean: As far as the overall presentation and construction of this USB flash drive goes, this drive is a solid product. It looks like the drive's body is made out of anodized aluminum and comes in gold color. I've been using similar drives for a couple of years now, having switched completely to small footprint/micro drives. They don't take up much space physically, don't rely on plastic bodies that tend to break over time, and don't have LED lights, which I find useless. Many reviewers have already pointed out the drive's design and water resistance feature (COB technology). Along with its physical features and reliability, I find it very important to test the drive's efficiency. The manufacturer did not list the read and write speed on the packaging itself so I used two different software products to perform several read/write speed tests, which produced the following results. USB speed test app #1 results: read: 42.6MB/s write: 28 MB/s read: 110 MB/s write: 34.7 MB/s read: 133 MB/s write: 52 MB/s read: 103 MB/s write: 32.5 MB/s USB speed test app #2 results: ReadTest: QT 1: 133.689 MB/s QT 2: 123.152 MB/s QT 3: 133.689 MB/s QT 4: 122.549 MB/s WriteTest: QT 1: 106.837 MB/s QT 2: 123.152 MB/s QT 3: 123.152 MB/s QT 4: 20.242 MB/s I'm not sure what caused such disparity in results but overall, the drive is moderately consistent when it comes to performance. Combined with the limited lifetime warranty, water resistance, low cost, excellent construction, this drive should be an excellent choice for anyone who's shopping for a portable external storage solution.

summary: It's working great for almost half a year
reviewText_clean: A rookie installed the wireless backup camera!!! It's working great for almost half a year. It went through the MN winter. Here I have my personal instructions for rookies like me. It will will you a general idea but you have to be careful at details!!! First, we need a backup camera, a wireless transmitter, a monitor, butt connectors, heat-sensitive insulators, zip ties, tools to open the truck screws, screw drivers, a electrical meter. Of course wires came with the camera. You will need a friend too. General scheme is: the camera and transmitter get power from backup light, the receiver and monitor get power from front ignition. Usually turn the key to ACC or ON is enough. In this case you car won't move but you still get electricity for the lights. Second, you will have to open up the truck and locate the backup light. Verify the positive and negative by a meter. Connect the positive wire from the light to positive wire from transmitter. Negative to negative. Connect the transmitter to the camera. Use butt connectors and insulators. Use zip ties and electrical types as well to guarantee they stay firm. Third, I bought a cigarette power from eBay so I will have 3 ports providing power. So I connected receiver and monitor to the ports. Same thing, positive to positive and negative to negative. Finally, you can try the rearview camera! It took a whole afternoon to figure out and another 2 hrs to install. Boy, really not easy...

summary: ONE OF THE BEST SOUNDING SOUNDBARS OUT THERE.  RICH CLEAR OPEN SOUND FOR VOICE, MOVIES, AND CASUAL MUSIC LISTENING.
reviewText_clean: Very Good Sound. Open, rich, natural, can be played loud, and NOT a little boxed in and lacking in the vocals in like my older Yamaha Sound Bar or even the newer ZVOX SB500 that I had at the same time and did an A-B With. The ZVOX sounded a little thin and tin like and slightly boxy to me compared to the richer more open sound of the Pioneer SP-SB23W. This Pioneer sound bar offers Optional bluetooth for your music, another setting for movies, and another setting for voice. The voice pretty much cuts the subwoofer, the music ads modest bass and subwoofer, and the movie seems to had more to the treble and the bass. The subwoofer is adjustable on all settings. I had a little trouble getting the subwoofer to sync at first. However, even though they originally ask you to push the button on the main soundbar and sub for them to sync originally, if you ever loose the sync with the subwoofer, you can unplug the subwoofer and just push the sync button on it without dealing with the main soundbar button again or maybe even wait and the sub syncs on its own later. By the way, I have a high end stereo system that I assembled over the years which will challenge most stereo systems around, and know good sound when I hear it. Bear in mind, no soundbar with its physical and design limitations will compare to a larger stereo system in quality. The design of the Pioneer is a little mousy and boring looking, but at a distance under the TV it looks fine and more importantly, for a soundbar, what you hear is one of the best soundbars out there. PERIOD. Why not. It has numerous larger drivers instead of tiny ones. The subwoofer is wireless and a little small, but for that reason, integrates better with the sound than some others easily produces rich deep bass (adjustable) for music and videos and being wireless lets you move it to an ideal location. I suspect that bigger is better and the physics of the larger speaker drivers in this sound bar and isolated amplifiers is what delivers the rich sound heard in comparison to other soundbars I have hear. I hear clear yet rich quality dialog and good dynamic response with movies and music. The Pioneer SB-SB23W allows you to use the Bluetooth function to control it with your iPad, phone, computer, etc. So if you have a library of digitized music on your computer or phone or want to use music and radio services to play through it, for its size, it will not disappoint and can fill your livingroom or even most of your house with sound. This soundbar will learn the buttons on your TV remote also. You just hold down the learn button until it flashes or turns solid blue, use the Pioneer remote and touch the key you want to program, then touch your corresponding remote key, they touch the pioneer one last time to program that key and continue through everything on your remote that you want to program, then hold down the learn key again until it stops flashing or turns solid blue which finalizes programming. I mention this because a u tube video by pioneer says to hold down the learn key until it turns a solid blue, and from my experience, a flashing blue is what you really get with my unit to trigger the learning mode. This subwoofer is being clearanced, so I assume a newer more modern one is coming out. However, don't assume it will sound as good or better, especially for the price. The trend is toward slimmer smaller soundbards with smaller speakers that can't match larger drivers in quality and volume of sound. My older Yamaha soundbar did not sound as good, and could not be played loud like this Pioneer sound bar. Bear in mind that CNET in its 2018 review, even with the new soundbars in place, still put this soundbar above most of the slightly more attractive newer more expensive and slimmer units sound wise. If you can get past some of the reliability complaints, this is one of the best sounding soundbars under $1,000 out there. There have been some complaints historically about reliability. Perhaps Pioneer has corrected these problems over time. I have had mine for about a month, and I have no problems. Perhaps buying this Pioneer SB23W at the discounted clearance price brand new and spending the extra $20 for the extended warranty is a very good idea. Another good idea, is to do as I have done and simply to leave it on even if muted at night for about two or three weeks straight. If there are any defects or if anything is going to go out , it will probably do it by then. Either way, know that although it is not the prettiest (nor is it ugly) or quit as fully featured as others , you are buying one of the best sounding sound bars out there for both music and movies at any price.

summary: ROUTER REFLECTIONS
reviewText_clean: Skiva 4-Port 802.11n N300 Wifi router with USB Storage Port (300 Mbps), WPS Button [Model:RT001 ] This router is AMAZING! With that said, let it be known that I received this router at a discount to give a FAIR & BALANCED REVIEW. Everything you need comes in the box and is simple to hook up. PLEASE SEE ATTACHED PICS. I am not a highly technical person, but have enough knowledge to do some computer techy stuff. However, installing this router wasn't as straightforward as it could have been. Instructions that come in the box in the form of a step-by-step diagram and on the mini CD were a bit ambiguous, but not impossible to navigate or understand. The CD would not auto run so I had to locate it (using File Explorer in Windows 10) and then click on AUTORUN.exe. A menu appeared entitled "Welcome to the Setup Guide" and then I clicked the START button. It stepped me through the process to connect the router, but it doesn't know your specific modem so it can't help you there. You should know where to hook up the cable to your modem. Then it auto checks your connections to make sure everything was done right. You can also use WPS which automatically finds your modem and devices (if your modem and devices have WPS as well). Once hooked up (I used WPS) everything functioned normally. I have several devices in my household (two laptops, 1 desktop, 4 cell phones [droid and iPhone] an iPad and an Amazon FIRE tablet). At least 4 of these various devices are running at any given time, and on occasion, when guests are here, there are more. One of the great features of this router is the built in USB port that allows you to connect USB storage devices, whether hard drives or flash drives, and share it with your entire home network with firewall security. I currently have a Netgear WND3700 Dual Band Router. As far as speed or range go, I couldn't tell the difference between the SKIVA and my NETGEAR. One of the capabilities of this router is the ability to connect as a 2nd router to extend your wireless range, however, you SHOULD NOT attempt to do this unless you know what you are doing. Have someone technical do this for you otherwise you may have conflicts and interference. I tested the SKIVA router by itself, but intend to use it as a range extender, so I will report back in a few weeks on how that works. I DO NOT foresee any problems. Regarding the FULL capabilities of this WIRELESS N router there are many advanced technical aspects that can be achieved for you "geeks" out there. I fully recommend this product whether you are a techy or just an average "joe" or "joan". The router I received is the latest version and does not have the problems or inconsistencies you may have read about in other reviews from the earlier product. This router has not dropped any signals and has not shown any undesirable characteristics with my setup. I use COMCAST and NETGEAR with DROID, WINDOWS and APPLE. There is technical support available from SKIVA online, in writing with the User Manual, or via landline phone number. This SKIVA router has a 1 year HASSLE FREE warranty.

summary: Glad I bought it! Was almost fun to install...BUT warranty service is costly
reviewText_clean: Updated 12/1/17: Ive had a problem with the camera not working, kept on struggling with re-soldering my connections to the back-up lamps wires, and just discovered the problem: the wires go to a small plug that plugs into a junction box that is wired to the camera. With vibration, the plug worked loose. Pushing it in again and taping it in place has fixed the issue. So this is now going strong around two years after purchase. UPDATED 9/23/16: Our monitor died. Power comes through the cord, but the monitor is dead. I contacted the company, and here's the warranty situation: I have to send this back, with copy of my receipt. That makes sense. But I also have to enclose a $15 money order or prepaid shipping label. That means it's going to cost me a bit over $20 for what I hope to be warranty replacement. This is not what I'd call a good deal. Just saying... and another update: 12/8/16: Well, I still don't like that it cost me $20 or so for the return, but they promptly shipped my monitor back, or maybe a new one, working better than before. Now after I back out of the driveway, I hit the power switch, and the monitor only rarely comes on when a spurious signal comes its way. This purchase had made backing up easier and safer. I'm glad I bought it. ------------ We recently were out of town and rented a car, and discovered what how useful a back-up camera is. Once we'd tried one, it was hard to back up without one. I checked with a local car-accessories dealer, and they had a nice option for about $300, and an additional $300 for installation. I looked over what it would take to install a wired camera in our '08 Honda Civic Hybrid, and really didn't want to take the time & trouble to run a wire. I can manage basic wiring, but have neither the time nor skills to tear up and replace molding all over my car's interior. So I researched our options, and this device seemed a good choice. One competing device has the advantage of digital rather than analog signal, but they seem to have a bad track record of non-waterproof cameras with poor response for customer service. Our camera arrived neatly packed in a display box, with instructions that were general but adequate. Installation was not difficult, but took a while. I had to open up the area of a backup light, and I chose to solder the two wires to the positive and negative wires. Another option would be quickie connectors one can buy at auto supply stores. Then I took off the license plate, reinstalled it with the camera in place, and ran the wire over to connect with the gadget that I wired into the taillight. Then it was simply a matter of plugging the plug of the monitor into the cigarette lighter socket, and clicking the monitor into the flexible mount. The build quality is excellent. The mount is solid, display sometimes a bit hard to see in bright light, but definitely adequate. The camera turns on when I switch into reverse, and the display is on in about 1 second, about as much time as it takes to release the emergency brake. The display gives me good visibility in daytime and twilight, and in the dark, the backup taillights provide enough light for the camera. Now the minor downsides: driving along in the day, if I leave the monitor on, it has a blue screen that says No Signal. Going by the occasional car or business that's sending the right signal, I'll get a brief flicker on the screen. At night, the blue screen is distracting. The fix: I hold down the power switch for a bit over a second, and the display shuts off. I don't think it's a full shutoff, it goes black with the occasional flicker as I describe above. And if I hit enough of a bump, the monitor does turn on, so I have to repeat the off-switch procedure. When I need it on, pushing the switch does the job, as will starting the car, and of course putting the car into reverse. The warranty on the unit is one year, and Pyle gives you a 3-month addition for writing a review. I did contact tech support about that bump-on issue, and got a rapid, helpful response. I'm really happy with this purchase. I think the value was great, quality seems good. It's good to have this for our Civic, which has pretty good rear-view visibility. Just tonight, I was backing up in a parking lot and the wide angle of the camera showed me two people about to walk behind our car--they were beyond the viewing angle of our mirror. With a van or SUV with limited rear-visibility, this is a safety necessity. ---Update: Still love the camera kit. There are times, e.g. around dusk, when objects behind the car seem really dark in the monitor, but it still seems adequate for safety. The one thing I wish is that it would stay dark when the gearshift is not in reverse. Best solution I've found at night is just to unplug the power cord that goes to the monitor.

summary: Using a paperclip is ridiculous
reviewText_clean: It was purchased as a gift for me by my daughter. We purchased it from Radio Shack in early 2015. I was really excited to get it. In the package was a large and small wrist band, the tracker and the metal fastener. In the beginning I had difficulty getting the tracker to charge. Of course I thought in the beginning it was my fault so I did all of the prescribed steps again and again and finally got it to charge long enough to use it. It lasted less than 2 days for the charge. So I tried again to get it to charge. It just would not work. So I packaged it back up in it's original package and put it in my closet. Everyone of my friends were using their Fitbit flex. Some had the same problem and others just stopped using it just as I did. But, three weeks ago I decided to try to use it again. Again it would not charge. I contacted the company for the fifth or 6th time. Again I am given the list of what to do. which of course it does not work. UpDate: Fitbit company contacted me regarding the issue. So they (the company) decided that it was out of warranty. So their solution was for me to purchase another Fitbit product at a discounted rate. So they the company wants me to spend more of my money. I would want to do that. WHY? Then I find a video on YouTube about how to use small paperclip and place it in the end of the tracker to push it down just enough to make contact in the charger. Guess what it works. (Which is absolutely ridiculous) . However,it has to be charged every 2 1/2 days which I don't believe is normal. So a year and a half later I am using it. With no help from the company. (The customer service is horrible) But, my daughter paid $99.00 for it. So I plan to get some use out of it. If at all possible. My point to all of this is. If you can not get it to charge after all the prescribed steps Fitbit the company tells you. Try a small paperclip, put it in the end of the tracker so it pushes the tracker down a little in the charger cradle. And watch to see if it works for you.
