summary: Great inexpensive earbuds
reviewText_clean: My husband uses these as almost "disposable" earbuds. He has tinnitus and requires blocking sound to get to sleep. As you can imagine, sleeping in earbuds isn't exactly taking good care of them, and things do happen....typically after a month or two he will lose sound in one ear or the other. To date, he's gone through probably a dozen pair of these over the past few years. However the price is so cheap, that's not a problem. The maker does issue a "lifetime warranty" on them but we've simply never tried to capitalize on that because of the way he uses them - it doesn't seem fair to them. The main thing I wanted to let folks know is that the newer version of these earbuds has an L shaped earphone jack instead of the straight jack, and that makes a world of difference in how long they are lasting him. Pay the extra buck or two for the ones where Amazon tells you "there is a newer version of this product available", if you end up searching and finding the older model. Both models (older and new) come with multiple sizes of the rubber ear stoppers and are great for normal use. I can't really comment on sound quality if that's a big concern for you, but overall they are definitely a solid earbud for standard purposes like listening to an MP3 player as you walk around or work out, commuting on public transport, etc.

summary: From washed out sickly images to vibrant hot colors in a couple of tweaks....Nikon D 750,  an awesome rig.
reviewText_clean: For any other person who has problems with 'washout', weak colors in images, misting and so on. I am not an Amazon buyer, and the Nikon D 750 I have is a refurb. Set up; Nikon D 750 and Nikon AF 50mm F i. 4 D lens. ( Same lens as was used in the initial 2014 advertising of the Nikon D 750 ) Getting to the point; my camera came configured for Video, i.e it is set up to make really nice video clips. Had to return it under warranty to fix a couple of odd things, horizon setting not coming on, and Fn assignment not working right. Got it back fixed and everything seems Ok except on wide shots, i.e buildings, landscape etc., and indoors with lighting, the colors are really weak with a bit of 'misting'; an overall sickly appearance. I discovered by fiddling with the menu settings that the solution lies in the 'Shooting' menu option, 'Set Picture Control' > 'SD Standard' > you, the reader, do these adjustments "sharpening from 3 up to 5" // " saturation from 0 up to 2 " // "hue from 0 up to 1". Must add that I checked these settings out in a darkened room with a spotlight, and to get the colors spot on - subject V Image - had to back off flash to -0.3, and select ISO 200. The latter had been set to 800 by auto ISO ! That tells how far off the sensors are. That fixes my image washout, and appears with much the same veracity as my old camera, Nikon D 90. (It just goes to show that today the old workhorses are still competitive with the new technology! ) However the D 90 is DX and needs really fancy glass to get some of the shots I need, while the D 750 can use older glass of the same, or better, quality, but at a tenth of the price. I was quite surprised at this outcome. So why not a kit lens? I do not use stills gear to make video, I use a dedicated Videocam for that. In fact I don't really need a G lens at all, except for long 'VR" type imaging, and I rarely to never need fast G lenses - F 2.8 etc - as I don't do low light at all even if I have some excellent primes for that sort of thing. Other glass tested on this rig, Ai S 105 MM F 2.8 Macro - it is absolutely perfect for nature/macro and then some. All of the above with the new tweaks will be as nice but far nicer with the stronger color saturation. Overall impression; for portraits/head shots this rig is the beesknees, nice long lens would be best here, eg an old workhorse like the Nikkor Ai S Telephoto 200mm F 4 . Too It really excels on Engineering and such, mostly with Nikon AF 50mm F 1.8 D lens, hardly ever need anything else on those. Forensic and Insurance 'quibble' type imaging goes down a bit, and for close up tis all stacking/Macro. In short if you are into techie stuff and not arty shots then this is the way to go. Obviously if you prefer arty photography you need the Nikon D 810, and some awesome glass. Other pluses for me, easy access to adjusting ISO, its on the back, Auto Focus, its on the AF button on side of camera, Metering, its on the top, and - in my case - 'Ai S' lens selection inbuilt program - on Fn Button ( had to program that myself ...lol ) I love the 'P' mode front wheel adjustment from full open / flat DOF / to full closed / tunnel DOF. None of these need going into the menu system to tweak. Then the swivel screen on back saves me having to get down on the ground /aim up/ or low, just fip into 'live view' and swing out the screen, then I can do the job by bending down, no crawling around on the floor any more...thank you Nikon! Overall I am impressed with all of the new adjustments available. I did consider the D 500, same price, but backed off because of no flash, and expensive lens options. Couple of notes for newbies. This is not a newbie camera, you should think about the D 7200, or the D 500, instead. There is nothing wrong with either of these as a starter DLSR camera, in fact I would love to have begun my DSLR days with the D 7200 rather than the D 90. But coming from FX analogue to digital FX is just too far a jump even for a lifetime shutter bug like me. But I am keeping my D 90, it does all my sales gigs, kit lens, and will continue to do so forever...lol

reviewText_clean: ** Update 3-22-17*** After multiple back and forth discussions with Peak Design's support team, and a 5 day wait since my last message to them, the customer service rep offered me a " maybe you have too much stuff in the side pocket." I carry an Olympus camera with a 12-40 pro lens and a 40-150 pro lens in the main bag, making it more than heavy enough to hold the bag upright with the exception the base is possibly too narrow by design or my particular bag is defective, neither of which customer service seems very interested in getting too excited about addressing or diagnosing. It is a shame that this beautiful bag with a lifetime warranty tips off of the back seat of the car if seated upright with my relatively light gear. *** Small Update*** - after using for approximately 3 months, there is only 1 downside to this item... the bag is a little "top heavy" when loaded and has a tendency to tip over due to a narrower base. Minor, but would suggest keeping the bag closed so gear does not tumble out This bag is a great size and weight for a mirrorless camera system or a smaller dslr. Works great for my Olympus OM-D EM-10 and lens system. Exterior of the bag has a great feel and pockets are set up well for extra batteries, airblower, small book, filters, etc. Even when filled up, the bag still keeps a sveldt footprint without smashing the gear. Would HIGHLY recommend watching the PEAK DESIGN TIPS AND TRICKS video (...) for the messenger bag in order to fully comprehend the catches, latches, and folding dividers. Only 1 criticism of this smaller version of the bag and that is they only include 2 dividers. I understand the the logic behind smaller bag, fewer dividers, but this bag is really in need of a 3rd divider. I did order one off of their website, but it is really a $20 add on as they charge a full $5.00 shipping for the $14.95 divider. Raise the price of the bag by $5 and include the 3rd divider. 4 is too many, 2 is too few. 3 dividers give the user the right number of options to section off the bag and also model the options given in the tutorial video.

reviewText_clean: I received this Buffalo LinkStation 420 4 TB 2-Drives NAS about 2 weeks ago to use with my IP Security Cameras. I tried to use WD MyCloud as A NAS but had nothing but problems. summary: Loses 2 stars for a lack of durability.
reviewText_clean: I had this machine about 19 months. Then the motherboard (or a component that is hard soldered to the motherboard) randomly blew out on me, rendering the machine dead. And it only has a 12 month warranty, so I was left with a nearly $700 paperweight less than 2 years after purchase. The machine is a superb 5 star machine when it worked. It's a 1 star useless piece of junk after it broke. I don't know how often the ZenBooks go bad. I do know that it happens enough that when I googled the problem I could find a ton of other people who had experienced the same issue. I have Dell and HP laptops that have worked for the better part of a decade. They are outdated but still power on and work as well as when they were new. So it's severely disappointing to me that my ZenBook broke in under 2 years and I was left with no warranty from ASUS. As for how well the machine worked prior to it dying..... DISPLAY The screen is great. I mean really great. It's a matte finish which REALLY cuts down on glare. I can sit with a bright light directly behind me and not see any reflection of the light at all. When I hold my phone at the same angle as my screen I can't see a thing on the phone screen (normal glossy smartphone screen). The resolution is fantastic, and even with the native display settings maximized for the HD screen resolution all the text is big enough to read comfortably. The bezel around the screen looks much bigger in the picture at the top of this page. It's really not that big and the actual LCD panel fills the screen area well. There is a rubber gasket all the way around the outer edge of the bezel that will do 2 things. It will keep the metal screen housing from rubbing against the metal keyboard housing and scratching them both up. It will also provide some (I said SOME) protection against water getting in if the lid is closed. This might come in handy if the Zenbook is in a backpack and you get caught in the rain. It's not waterproofing. It's "buy you 20 seconds to run inside" protection. There is an issue with the back of the lip lifting the machine up a little when the screen is opened all the way which can cause scratching on wooden surfaces. I don't like this design choice. KEYBOARD Prior to this machine I'd been using 2 keyboards regularly. A Dell Latitude D630 notebook keyboard that is full size with normal laptop keys, and a full size normal desk top keyboard with big keys. Both have 'normal' key travel. The Zenbook is my first island key set up. It took me about 8 seconds to get used to it. The key travel isn't as deep as my Dell Latitude keyboard, but it's not much more shallow. It's very easy to type on. The Power button being above the backspace key and built into the keyboard seems to be a big issue with a lot of people. I type like The Thing from the Fantastic Four (Big dude made of orange rock) so I have already used the backspace key a lot in the last 2 hours. I haven't hit the power button yet. I also think it gives the whole system a nice clean look that there isn't a row of system buttons above the function key row. The trackpad. Yes, it clicks a little when you tap it. Yes, it was annoying for the first hour. I got used to it as soon as I realized it wasn't broken. It dose that because the whole trackpad is a clickable button. So there is play in the trackpad. It's not loud. It's not wiggling loose. It's just not a big deal. SPEAKERS The speakers are on the bottom. To be more specific they are on the very sides of the bottom and angled slightly out toward the sides. They aren't full size JBL tower speakers that will wake up the neighbors, but they aren't trying to be. They are quiet laptop speakers. And the volume they are capable of varies. I actually have 2 ZenBookk UX305's. One for me and one for my wife. Mine, prior to it's untimely demise, had okay volume. It was audible but not loud. My wife's machine is REALLY quiet and the speakers are generally useless. Same model machine. INTERNAL GEEKY STUFF I can't slow this system down. I've thrown all my normal usage stuff at it (Office, web browsing...with multiple java heavy tabs, watching videos, etc etc) and I can't slow it down. The 8GB of RAM is more than enough for 95% of users. Maybe it wouldn't make a great video editing machine, but the vast majority of the world isn't ever going to do that. If you're doing resource intensive stuff you know you need a bigger more powerful machine and you're probably not looking at this one. The 256 SSD drive is amazing. When it says fast access it's not screwing around. It boots fast, wakes from sleep fast, and accesses files fast. This is all because the SSD storage lets the system quickly save and retrieve data. If you're a computer person you understand what I'm saying. If you're not, trust me. It's awesome. I actually saved the SSD drive off my dead ZenBook and put it into a case for M.2 style drives so I could keep the extra storage via USB to my new machine. It works great in that way too. And the hard drive is completely upgradable if you ever want to install a bigger drive. It's an M+B style connector on an M.2 drive. It's easy to remove it and replace it if you open up the machine. LOOK AND FEEL It's thin. Like crazy thin. With the lid closed the whole system is just a hair thicker than my Galaxy Tab 2 tablet. You hear what I'm saying? This nicely powered ultrabook computer is basically as thin as a very nice smartphone. That's insane to me. And it doesn't feel flimsy as a result. I was worried it would feel like I was going to break it in half because it's so thin. It feels pretty strong and sturdy. The all aluminum frame just feels expensive. (I mean the Zenbook isn't cheap, but it's not priced like a Mac Book either.) It's also very light. This is a double edged sword. The ONLY thing that's even remotely an issue with the Zenbook. When sitting on your lap the system bounces around as you type a little bit. It just doesn't have enough mass to keep it firmly planted on your lap. It's not a big deal, but it's noticeable compared to my old heavy 2007 Dell notebook. One the flip side, its ULTRA portable. It can sit on my lap all day and it'll never start to get heavy. It's quiet. Dead quiet. Ninjas could check their email in the middle of a mission and it wouldn't give them away. It's cold. It doesn't get warm. The aluminum body does a great job of dissipating the small amount of heat the builds up. THE FINAL VERDICT I dunno....it's a great machine when it works. I've bought 2 of them. One for me and one for my wife. My wife's is still working fine and I'm still happy with that one. And I was tried to buy a 3rd to replace my broken one, so obviously I'm feeling like mine breaking was a fluke and not common, but Amazon sent me the ZenBook Flip UX360 instead by mistake and I like that one too so I kept it. I recommend considering the ZenBook Flip for the better speakers and the ability to open the screen lid to a greater angle. The downside of the Flip is that the screen is glossy due to it being a touchscreen so there are reflections on it. Internally it's virtually identical to the UX305 ZenBook. The ONLY thing that gives me reservations about this machine at all is that 1 of the 2 of them I bought died in under 2 years. That durability scares me.

summary: Terrific personal radio. Highly recommend
reviewText_clean: This is a great little personal radio with stable reception and 10 FM presets. It replaced an old analog Sony that I used when I walked and lost (Of course, I found it after I ordered this one) But this has presets and two features (other than it's digital and has presets) that I really like. You can lock the buttons so that they can't be accidentally changed by hitting something in your pocket and it defaults to turning itself off after 90 minutes, which can be over-ridden by holding the power on button for a few extra seconds when turning it on. I would recommend it whole heartedly. I really like this radio. ***UPDATE**** April 10, 2016 I have really enjoyed this radio for all the reasons the reviewers have noted: easy to use; digital; 15 presets; button locking. etc. Up to now. I usually take this on my walks and went to use it today, and it was dead. I thought it was odd, since I had just replaced the batteries a few days ago after my last walk. I replaced the batteries and tried again, and again, it was dead. I looked in the manual and found a means to reset it. That didn't work either. This thing is just dead. I can assure you, that it was not abused. It hasn't moved from my desk since my last walk, when it worked fine. So I went online to see what the warranty is on this and it's 90 days. However, not only do you have to ship it back to them in California at your expense, but there's an $8 fee fpr them to fix or replace it under warranty. It was $32 on Amazon. Not a great buy if you have to add another $12+. I am very disappointed as I really liked this radio. It's the weekend, so I will call on Monday and see what they have to say for themselves. I'm hoping they have good customer support, as it's just under 90 days from when I got this on Jan. 21, 2016. ***UPDATE*** April 13 I called them and the tech I spoke to said to leave the batteries out for a day to see it would re-set itselt. It turns out, it was a much simpler fix than that. I use rechargeable batteries. It turns out, one of them was bad. It had nothing to do with the radio; it works just fine, as it always has. I thought I had put in a different set of batteries, but I didn't, so this is my fault. I would definitely recommentd this and their tech support was very helpful in tracking down the problem.

reviewText_clean: This was from UTM Inc. fulfilled by Amazon and presented as a U.S. Version. Although neither Amazon nor UTM acknowledged their mistake they both suggested I return the camera. I'm giving it 3 stars because I didn't have the camera long enough for solid feedback and Amazon and UTM made the camera and warranty easy to return. The warranty got processed right away, but I'm still waiting on the camera refund. I was also able to return the CompactFlash without a problem or fee. I only used the 7D for a few hours but I noticed: -there was one image taken indoors w/the pop up flash of the cat that my old T3i couldn't match (which might not sound like much but the T3i was/is a great entry level camera) -the autofocus was problematic (I couldn't see the image in focus through the viewfinder) -it was heavy -the layout on the left and dial and joystick on the right were awkward (my cousin's Canon has this same layout and she likes it, so...) -the menu and functions were close enough to my old EOS to quickly figure out -it was easy to find a YouTube video to help me change the language to English -Amazon had a link to the manual in English -there was no improvement in tricky outdoor sun and shadow shots -I didn't use it long enough for a good assessment but it felt clunky. Some of the outdoor photos were okay and one indoor was almost good enough to convince me to keep the camera I decided to return it because the seller seemed adamant that I do so. UTM didn't try to work with me (I sent three emails which they answered in good time) and they do NOT HAVE A WORKING PHONE NUMBER. The Amazon Chat rep was mostly unhelpful but did want to help me with a return (after I said I may want to keep it). He wouldn't help in reporting the product misrepresentation or non-functioning phone number. I should have at least gotten a link or number to report both. I've done more research and if I wasn't on a budget I'd look at the 5D or a Nikon. summary: Okay earbuds for sound quality but goodish for noise canceling
reviewText_clean: I have owned Bose QC20 for a week now. I listen to them at work in a factory. I've read tons of review on earbuds for under 300 and base off that I bought this. BTW I used them 10hrs a day. PROS: Sound is good at midrange to highrange. Silicone tips are super comfy. Wire from battery box to the y split is beefy. L shape jack. This is sturdier the straight jack. Noise cancelling works well for low pitch sound. Battery life exceeds 10hrs. Trusted brand name. Bass is good enoughish, could be better. CONS: Noise cancel does deliver a slight pressure like if you were going down a mountain and the attitude changes. 1 year warranty is BS from Bose, it should be 2 years at least. Earbuds wire to Y wire is thin and the battery box to the jack is even thinner, probably going to break. No claim on stress test (e.g. 10k bend test) Battery box can get awkward if you have small pockets. Price at $250, sound does not match the price tag if we are only talking about sound quality not NC. Sound quality without NC is mediocre. Carry case is too small causes you to wonder if you should use it cause of the sharp wire bends. FINAL THOUGHTS: Who is this for? People who want active noise canceling that don't mind a little pressure. I find the pressure to be bondersome and while it does block out most of the sound at a factory it does not justify the annoyance of the pressure. BTW I work night shift so my work place isn't as loud as you would think. I hope this will last me at least 2 years. I highly doubt it but we will see. I might return it before 30 days are over or I might keep it. I hope that pressure on the NC will dissipate with use.

summary: A Consumer-Friendly Sound in a (hopefully) Durable Package
reviewText_clean: My review of the Brainwavz Jive is originally posted on Head-Fi. First off, thanks to Pandora from Brainwavz for reaching out and offering the opportunity to look at the "Jive". Secondly, I noticed a trend that I'm giving 4 stars to everything I've reviewed so far haha. Am I too forgiving or too harsh? I don't even know! Intro: Still trying to get this "intro" part right, but basically I love music and headphones/IEMs. Definitely not an audiophile in any means, but I don't think that disqualifies me from being able to tell whether or not I like a headphone or not (I mean I hope not haha). I listen to a little bit of everything, but my playlist consists mostly of Pop, Punk, J-Pop/J-Rock, Electronic, and Hip-Hop. Onto the review! Information on Specs, microphone & remote, and included accessories were copied and pasted from Brainwavz Audios website. Specifications: Drivers : Dynamic, 9 mm Rated Impedance : 16 Frequency Range : 20 Hz ~ 20 kHz Sensitivity : 98 dB @ 1 mW Rated Input Power : 20 mW Plug : 3.5 mm, Gold-Plated Cable : 1.3 m, Copper Microphone & Remote: Phone Call Control Audio Player Control 3-Button Remote Supports TRRS Connector Supports Apple iOS and Android Devices Included Accessories: Earphone Hardcase (wide) 3 sets of Silicone Ear Tips (S M L) 1 set of Comply Foam Tips S-400 1 Shirt Clip Velcro Cable Tie Instruction Manual Warranty Card (24 month warranty) First Impressions Notes: -Driver flex -Bassy, somewhat harsh in the upper mids section -Dry midrange -Sweet hardshell carrying case Build/Design: Brainwavz claims that they are made out of high quality metal. The shiny finish seems to give off the look that they are metal, but they feel like hard plastic to me. I don't mind, but they still look nice. These don't stick out of my ears much and they haven't fallen out of my ears yet once Ive inserted them; but then again I like to insert IEMs deeper into the canal. I like the added cable cinch to help with tangling though it only goes up until the microphone. The strain relief between the housing and the cable seems to be very stiff though. Also, the color "blue" seems to be off.. I don't think I'm color blind but these look more purple in person than blue. Cable: The cable feels slightly rubberized and thick enough to not feel cheap. Even at that, I did not experience much microphonics if there were any at all. The Y-splitter is a great balance between being light weight and durable. The lower half of the cable is thicker and terminates into a 45 degree angle 3.5mm plug. 3-Remote Microphone: NOTE: I have contacted Brainwavz about the 3-button remote as I think I got the IOS version; I was told that the 3-button remote works for both Android and IOS. It does not work on my Sony Xperia Z3V and so I will not be able to fully review the 3-button remote. The middle button works as a play and pause button. There is also a volume up and down on it, but those unfortunately did not work during use. Isolation/Fit: Upon insertion, I can hear quite of bit of driver flexing where it sounds like something is crinkling inside of the IEMs. I don't seem to see any ports on the housings so Im assuming thats the reason to why there is quite a bit of driver flexing. As for isolation, these isolate very well. I used these in the kitchen the other day and only barely hearing the water running from the sink. I did use them at a fairly high listening level (say like 75%-85% on my phone) so that definitely played a role. As a reference, these isolated quite a bit better than my ATH-CKR10. These fit snugly into my ears with the provided medium tips. I did not experience any discomfort at all. Sound: Note: These have been burned in for about 40 hours. I think this is a necessary step for some IEMs, but since its for a review I do it anyway. Bass: Quite elevated and extends down low quite well. I could definitely feel the rumble of the sub-bass and the bass gives a satisfying amount of authority in the music. Although at times I found it a touch too much energy. Its great for electronic, hip-hop, rock, and pop; but I found the mid-bass to be a bit too prominent for my liking though. Its fun at times and at other times, I find myself making faces at how the bass is too strong. Mids: I think its a bit recessed in the lower half, but gradually rises giving this sense of shimmer in female vocals. I find this similar to how Audio Technica usually voices their headphones, though in return some could find it somewhat harsh, nasal, and unnatural sounding. If you know me, I really like how Audio Technica sounds especially in the mids so I don't mind this as much. Treble: Somewhat smooth and maybe a touch recessed in the high treble. I wish there was a little more clarity in the treble without crossing the lines of being sibilant and speaking of which I did not find these to be sibilant. I didn't find them to be very veiled sounding, but I wished it extended a little more as well. If you're that person who found the HD600 veiled, then uhh.. you probably would think these are also veiled sounding. Soundstage: Theres a decent amount of separation, but not nearly as much width to back it up. Its not going to take you to a different planet, thats for sure. Leave that to speakers. Conclusion: For 25 bucks (at the moment on Amazon), I think its a great deal. A consumer friendly sound fitted in a durable and light package with a remote (if you get it working) as a bonus with a hardshell carrying case, it's really hard not to like these! First off, thanks to Pandora from Brainwavz for reaching out and offering the opportunity to look at the "Jive". Secondly, I noticed a trend that I'm giving 4 stars to everything I've reviewed so far haha. Am I too forgiving or too harsh? I don't even know! Intro: Still trying to get this "intro" part right, but basically I love music and headphones/IEMs. Definitely not an audiophile in any means, but I don't think that disqualifies me from being able to tell whether or not I like a headphone or not (I mean I hope not haha). I listen to a little bit of everything, but my playlist consists mostly of Pop, Punk, J-Pop/J-Rock, Electronic, and Hip-Hop. Onto the review! Information on Specs, microphone & remote, and included accessories were copied and pasted from Brainwavz Audios website. Specifications: Drivers : Dynamic, 9 mm Rated Impedance : 16 Frequency Range : 20 Hz ~ 20 kHz Sensitivity : 98 dB @ 1 mW Rated Input Power : 20 mW Plug : 3.5 mm, Gold-Plated Cable : 1.3 m, Copper Microphone & Remote: Phone Call Control Audio Player Control 3-Button Remote Supports TRRS Connector Supports Apple iOS and Android Devices Included Accessories: Earphone Hardcase (wide) 3 sets of Silicone Ear Tips (S M L) 1 set of Comply Foam Tips S-400 1 Shirt Clip Velcro Cable Tie Instruction Manual Warranty Card (24 month warranty) First Impressions Notes: -Driver flex -Bassy, somewhat harsh in the upper mids section -Dry midrange -Sweet hardshell carrying case Build/Design: Brainwavz claims that they are made out of high quality metal. The shiny finish seems to give off the look that they are metal, but they feel like hard plastic to me. I don't mind, but they still look nice. These don't stick out of my ears much and they haven't fallen out of my ears yet once Ive inserted them; but then again I like to insert IEMs deeper into the canal. I like the added cable cinch to help with tangling though it only goes up until the microphone. The strain relief between the housing and the cable seems to be very stiff though. Also, the color "blue" seems to be off.. I don't think I'm color blind but these look more purple in person than blue. Cable: The cable feels slightly rubberized and thick enough to not feel cheap. Even at that, I did not experience much microphonics if there were any at all. The Y-splitter is a great balance between being light weight and durable. The lower half of the cable is thicker and terminates into a 45 degree angle 3.5mm plug. 3-Remote Microphone: NOTE: I have contacted Brainwavz about the 3-button remote as I think I got the IOS version; I was told that the 3-button remote works for both Android and IOS. It does not work on my Sony Xperia Z3V and so I will not be able to fully review the 3-button remote. The middle button works as a play and pause button. There is also a volume up and down on it, but those unfortunately did not work during use. Isolation/Fit: Upon insertion, I can hear quite of bit of driver flexing where it sounds like something is crinkling inside of the IEMs. I don't seem to see any ports on the housings so Im assuming thats the reason to why there is quite a bit of driver flexing. As for isolation, these isolate very well. I used these in the kitchen the other day and only barely hearing the water running from the sink. I did use them at a fairly high listening level (say like 75%-85% on my phone) so that definitely played a role. As a reference, these isolated quite a bit better than my ATH-CKR10. These fit snugly into my ears with the provided medium tips. I did not experience any discomfort at all. Sound: Note: These have been burned in for about 40 hours. I think this is a necessary step for some IEMs, but since its for a review I do it anyway. Bass: Quite elevated and extends down low quite well. I could definitely feel the rumble of the sub-bass and the bass gives a satisfying amount of authority in the music. Although at times I found it a touch too much energy. Its great for electronic, hip-hop, rock, and pop; but I found the mid-bass to be a bit too prominent for my liking though. Its fun at times and at other times, I find myself making faces at how the bass is too strong. Mids: I think its a bit recessed in the lower half, but gradually rises giving this sense of shimmer in female vocals. I find this similar to how Audio Technica usually voices their headphones, though in return some could find it somewhat harsh, nasal, and unnatural sounding. If you know me, I really like how Audio Technica sounds especially in the mids so I don't mind this as much. Treble: Somewhat smooth and maybe a touch recessed in the high treble. I wish there was a little more clarity in the treble without crossing the lines of being sibilant and speaking of which I did not find these to be sibilant. I didn't find them to be very veiled sounding, but I wished it extended a little more as well. If you're that person who found the HD600 veiled, then uhh.. you probably would think these are also veiled sounding. Soundstage: Theres a decent amount of separation, but not nearly as much width to back it up. Its not going to take you to a different planet, thats for sure. Leave that to speakers. Conclusion: For 25 bucks (at the moment on Amazon), I think its a great deal. A consumer friendly sound fitted in a durable and light package with a remote (if you get it working) as a bonus with a hardshell carrying case, it's really hard not to like these! Sources: Sony Xperia Z3V 320 kbps MP3 and FLAC files

summary: Awesome but pricey.
reviewText_clean: tl;dr Amazing, well built monitor. I've had no issues, and the display is incredible. The joke reviews are kind of annoying; if you look at other 32" 4k IPS monitors, this one is a few hundred dollars overpriced at the time of this writing, but you get gsync. If you're a gamer, that might be worth it, if not, then don't buy it. Firstly the monitor is big. I have 30" monitors, and it even looks big compared to those. No matter how much space you're prepared for it to take up on your desk, chances are it's going to take more. For my eyes, this is the right size for 4k resolution. I can still read the text on the screen. I might have won the monitor lottery, but I have no dead pixels, no glaring light bleed, the color isn't obviously un-uniform. However, I'm a programmer and I don't see things the same way an artist would. I haven't even color calibrated the monitor in any way, so take these observations with the appropriate grains of salt; someone with more of an artist's eyes may find lots of things wrong. However, this is as nice as any monitor I've ever seen; it looks as good as my wife's retina iMac, just bigger. Game frame rates are silky smooth on my system. The monitor doesn't have an annoying glossy display, but it still reflects a little bit. Aesthetically, it looks a lot better in person than it does in pictures. I thought I was going to hate the stand and the logo; in person they're much more subdued, and I won't be replacing the stand. There's also a USB 3.0 port and some speakers I won't be using. The whole monitor feels solid, from its construction to the stand. And Acer is backing it up with a three year warranty, so hopefully if something goes wrong it will happen then. Pros Gorgeous display. Lots of space Silky smooth look in games if you're in the nvidia camp (if not, why are you looking at this monitor?) Not as ugly looking as I feared. Well constructed Cons Pricey; you have to really want a 4k IPS monitor with gsync to buy this one. Need to have a recent nvidia graphics card to fully appreciate. It's Acer... my last monitors were Dells and they've lasted nearly a decade. I don't have the same confidence that this acer will last that long, but time will tell. I'll update in the future if anything goes wrong or if I have more thoughts.

reviewText_clean: I purchased a brand new Sony FDR-AX33 4K handycam about 8 month ago (September, 2015). I am an avid photographer and videographer, and to be separated from my device at the beginning of summer hurts a lot. The Costco technical employee that connected me with Sony and helped arranging the repair process was excellent. However, I am posting this review, so that, others may know about the flushing purple defect with the Sony FDR-AX33 (that may emerge several month after using the device). Others have also reported the problim and believe it is a defect with the sensor in some batches. Finally, the FDR-AX33 handycam that I got also has some focusing issues when it is fully zoomed on far objects, but, I could live with that.

summary: Fantastic DVR, much better than what cable companies provide
reviewText_clean: In 2001, we got our first Tivo recorder. It was amazing to be able to schedule recordings from the program guide and record shows without the hassles of tapes, but still have the ease of fast forwarding. By 2004, HDTVs had started to become a norm, and our cable company offered DVR service for $11.95 a month - cheaper than Tivo's service- while being able to record two shows at once. A better product at a lower price became available, and we switched. What happened between 2004 and 2015? The cable company failed to iterate the hardware or experience in any substantial way. Meanwhile, Tivo had to reinvent themselves to compete. And that they did. The Roamio easily and handily beats the DVR it replaced (Scientific Atlanta 8300HD) in almost every aspect. An elephant in the room is cost. The Roamio Pro is more than $400 generally; first year service included, $150/yr thereafter. You have the upfront investment in the hardware is one thing to swallow, but the cost calculation is not easy. My cable company charges $8/mo for plain cable boxes, and $20/mo for non-multiroom DVRs. This pegs the cost for two years for one DVR at about $480. Thus, on cost alone, the Tivo is a losing proposition, costing $600 for two years versus $480 for the cableco DVR (granted, the Tivo is a massively better product for several reasons I'll elaborate on later.) However, the Roamio has six tuners. It can do a combination of watching and recording six shows at once. And you can buy a  TiVo Mini with RF Remote (Current Version) . This hooks up to another TV via ethernet (plug in internet) or coaxial (e.g. traditional cable box screw-on cord). These go from $90 refurbished to $120 new (generally), and have lifetime free service. They can watch live TV, recorded programs, or streaming services you are subscribed to (Netflix, Amazon, Hulu Plus, etc.). Once you factor that each Tivo Mini is essentially a multiroom DVR into the equation, and costs much less with no ongoing service fee, the value proposition changes. We rented four HD DVRs for the past ten years at $20/mo. The breakeven on the Tivo is less than ten months. The only cost from the cable company is $2 for a cablecard, and that's essentially a wash because going from four DVRs to one CableCard also eliminated the $1.50/mo additional outlet fee from our bill. So depending on your cost and your service expectation, you can easily save money buying a Tivo - depending on what your cableco charges, and the number of boxes. In regards to the setup: It's pretty good, with occasional quirks. Tivo hardware in all forms still has a slow boot time (then again, hardware from the cable company was never a champion in this area). The guided setup is pretty good, expect a couple reboots. The box in the settings walks you through setting it up. You do need to register the Tivo's serial number on the website before actually plugging it in though, otherwise the connection to the Tivo service will fail. Once it's done, the Tivo generally runs itself, automatically getting program guide information, automatically recording suggestions (unless you disable it, more on that later), doing a good job of tracking first runs of shows and recording only new episodes from the season you ask for onwards, etc. Hardware: Well designed, quiet, looks attractive. The main Roamio Pro box has a button that is a "Remote finder"; the remote will play a jingle until the button is pressed so you can find it. The remote is smaller than most cable company remotes but well laid out. It uses radio frequency in addition to infrared, so you don't need to have line of sight to the DVR for commands to go through. User experience: Good. It was almost sort of comforting that the sounds that played in 2001 on my first Tivo are the same sounds for commands on the new one. That's not to say they're outdated. Menus are intuitive and very fast. Changing channels does take 1-2 seconds (about on par for the cableco DVR it replaced). Guide, pause, rewind, fast forward, etc. are all essentially instantaneous, even on remote Tivo devices within the home. Tivo's OnePass is great with a couple exceptions (just be careful on the channel you pick and select include streaming: no if you want to prefer recordings to the local drive over online services that you may not subscribe to). Suggestions works well to record programs that Tivo thinks you may like (based on other programs you record and rate). It's not perfect but more input (thumbs up/down) trains it and it picks up stuff you'd never record on your own. Suggestions can be disabled, but since they will always be lowest priority (vs. need for live TV and programs you actually asked for it to record, deleted automatically if space is needed) there's no real reason to disable it. Storage: My previous cable box had room for 20 hours of HD content. The Roamio Pro can do 450 hours in HD, and it's multiroom, so in order to watch the show in one room and resume it in another, I don't need to record it more than once. Storage is also expandable via USB or eSATA. I haven't needed to do so yet. Reliability: I've only had mine for two months but all is well. My Tivo Series1 was a trooper for many years and was retired for cost savings, not failure. If you're on non-lifetime service, Tivo will replace boxes outside of warranty for $49, which mitigates the risk of hardware failure financially. The Tivo Minis have no moving parts and are thus less likely to fail. Streaming: Works fantastically in the home. Also works well outside, but be aware that any premium channel (HBO, Showtime, etc.) sets a flag on their channels that prevents streaming from the Roamio to your smartphone or tablet. You can download shows/movies from these premium channels to store on your phone/tablet and watch offline (planes, cars, etc.) later, but you must do the download to the device while at home. Overall, I can highly recommend the Roamio Pro. If you're looking at it from a pure money saving perspective, consider the cost per regular cable box rental, the cost of DVR rental (if that is a priority) vs. hardware cost of Tivo, the cost of Tivo service after the first year, cablecard rental fee, etc... but the user experience is also much, much better. The only thing you really lose versus a cable company box is the use of ondemand (Comcast subscribers can use on demand with Tivo). With six tuners to record whatever your household wants, this is probably much less of an issue. If you're looking to use Minis with your Tivo, the main gotcha is they can't work wirelessly, and must use either ethernet or coaxial cable for networking (see my review on the Tivo Mini for details). They really are what makes the Roamio a great DVR if you have more than one cable box in your household.

Storage: My previous cable box had room for 20 hours of HD content. The Roamio Pro can do 450 hours in HD, and it's multiroom, so in order to watch the show in one room and resume it in another, I don't need to record it more than once. Storage is also expandable via USB or eSATA. I haven't needed to do so yet. Reliability: I've only had mine for two months but all is well. My Tivo Series1 was a trooper for many years and was retired for cost savings, not failure. If you're on non-lifetime service, Tivo will replace boxes outside of warranty for $49, which mitigates the risk of hardware failure financially. The Tivo Minis have no moving parts and are thus less likely to fail. Streaming: Works fantastically in the home. Also works well outside, but be aware that any premium channel (HBO, Showtime, etc.) sets a flag on their channels that prevents streaming from the Roamio to your smartphone or tablet. You can download shows/movies from these premium channels to store on your phone/tablet and watch offline (planes, cars, etc.) later, but you must do the download to the device while at home. Overall, I can highly recommend the Roamio Pro. If you're looking at it from a pure money saving perspective, consider the cost per regular cable box rental, the cost of DVR rental (if that is a priority) vs. hardware cost of Tivo, the cost of Tivo service after the first year, cablecard rental fee, etc... but the user experience is also much, much better. The only thing you really lose versus a cable company box is the use of ondemand (Comcast subscribers can use on demand with Tivo). With six tuners to record whatever your household wants, this is probably much less of an issue. They really are what makes the Roamio a great DVR if you have more than one cable box in your household.

summary: Works fine as expansion drive for my PS4
reviewText_clean: This review is for the 8TB hard drive. Included with the external hard drive are the instructions, a power cord, approximately 65 inches in length and a 3.0 USB cable, approximately 45 inches in length. This is one of the few times that I don't have to complain about short cables provided with external drives as these are plenty long enough. I got this drive to use as extended storage for my PS4. I have previously been using the Seagate Expansion 1TB external drive for extended storage but after a recent game buying splurge, I have run out of space with that drive. I have two of those drives and both are approximately three years old ago and are still going strong (one as the PS4 drive and one as a security cam drive) with no issues. Both of those drives were great for portability as well because of their small size. This 8 TB isn't quite as portable as the smaller Seagate drives at approximately 7 inches by 5 inches by 2-inch thickness and this drive requires a power supply unlike the smaller drives but considering the space that this has and that it is primarily being used on my PS4, it is less of an issue. Like all extended storage drives for the PS4, it has to be formatted by the PS4 but that is quick and painless to do. The transfer of files from my main PS4 and the 1 TB drive to this drive took a bit of time but that is mainly because there is no easy way to move the game files from expansion drive to another expansion drive in the PS4. The file transfer was fairly speedy otherwise. I have use a variety of brand name drives, including WD, Toshiba and these Seagates. I have not had any issues with either the Seagate drives or the WD as they both make very reliable drives and I expect the same from this drive. With this drive priced at about 18 dollars per TB, it is a reasonable cost for this size drive. Although I am not using it for that purpose, with this drive being USB 3.0, I expect this is just as speedy as most USB 3.0 drives on a Windows based computer. This has a power/hard drive light in the back-left side of the case. Although I am not personally a fan of the light in the back, it does make it less distracting and since I am using this as a drive for the PS4, being able to see the light isn't a huge issue. Oddly, these drives only have 1-year warranty, unlike the 1TB Seagate expansions that I bought that had 3-year warranties. Maybe that is a trend with manufacturers for lesser warranties, but I hope that doesnt indicates its drive reliability. I will update my review if I have any issues with durability. Overall, I like the drive for my PS4 expansion drive and it is so far working as it should with no slow down or stuttering when playing a variety of games. 4 stars

summary: Beautiful speaker, Beautiful sound.
reviewText_clean: . The sound quality is comparable to  Harman Kardon Onyx Studio 2  and almost as good as my $400 home stereo speakers (Cambridge SoundWorks). Impressive. It looks and feels like A quality. If you like its appearance in photos, you will probably fall in love with it when you hold it and inspect it close up. It lacks some controls and displays that other speakers have. I think GGMM is aiming for clean and simple. This is my initial reviewmore to come. - - - Disclosure - - - The manufacturer gave me this item for review. I believe my review is impartial. - - - Sound quality - - - The first thing I noticed: tunes with acoustic bass sound great. The bass notes (40 to 150 Hz) come through fully (see Note 2). The mids and highs are good too. The highs might be the weak point for serious listeners. This is where I noticed some difference vs my home stereo system. PROs: * Clean + Retro design that could win an award * Looks and feels like quality in almost every detail (See Note 1). * Bass is very good - Acoustic bass (instrument) plays beautifully (see Note 2). * Sound quality seems very good for the speakers size and price (see above). - Volume - Claimed 40 Watt output seems about right. I was able to listen at a 70-ft distance outdoors (see Note 3). - No audio delay using Bluetooth! (matters when watching video). (0.02 sec or less. See Note 4.) - Bluetooth range - Tested out fine at 70ft clear path outdoors (see Note 5). - Many speakers can work together in WiFi Mode. Did not try. But I had drop-outs in WiFi Mode. - 3-year warranty CONs: * WiFi (Router mode) has too many drop-outs for me (see Note 6). (Also, there is a continual .25 second sound delay not good for video sync.) - - - Features not included - - - I like that its not too cluttered with displays and controls. But missing features might bother you. - No microphone (for taking phone calls) - No equalizer (except for bass boost button) - No control of the source device (pause, next track, etc.) Also, It does not manipulate the source devices volume control. The M4 adds its own volume control to the pipeline. When playing music from my Mac, Im dealing with 3 volume controls in series (iTunes volume, Mac volume, and M4 volume). NIT PICKs: - A Volume knob would be nice instead of volume buttons. - Mode light uses white = Bluetooth, blue = WiFi. Blue for Bluetooth might be more expected. - Mine came with no User Manual. Just a fluke, I suppose. - - - Size and Weight - - - 4.5 x 6.2 x 14.3 6.3 lbs. - - - Notes - - - Note 1: Quality look & feel - If you look very closely, the quality of materials and construction is even more impressive. I found one flaw, but a very picky one...almost nobody will notice it. Note 2: Bass - I have a lot of tunes featuring an acoustic bass. The bass lines are strong and beautiful on the M4. I also tested with a tone generator (YouTube). Sound starts tailing off around 60 Hz (claimed cut-off for this speaker) but tones as low as 35-40 Hz are somewhat audible.) I found no use for the Bass Boost button. In one situation (inside my travel van) the bass was too strong. I wished for a reduce bass button. Note 3: Volume - Music was listenable at 70 ft. distance on outdoor patio. Some concrete guiding the sound. Light traffic noise in background. Note 4: Audio delay - It matters when watching movies, TV, YouTube, or any type of video, if lips and words are too far removed. Most Bluetooth speakers and headphones I've tested have a .08 to .13 second delay, which your brain will find acceptable when watching video. This has .02 seconds delay or less using Bluetooth. Impressive. WiFi connection (via WiFi router) is .25 seconds too delayed for use with video. Note 5: Bluetooth Range - Tested with iPhone 6. Range depends on both sending and receiving devices. I did not test at greater than 70 ft. I also tested holding the phone behind my back: Started skipping out at 15-20 feet. Note 6: Skips in WiFi (Router) mode - I tested this a few times. I got 2-4 second drop-puts at random times. Sometimes one every 5-15 minutes. Sometimes more often. Sometimes less often. Not sure whos to blame or if you will have the same problem. My WiFi ac router is D-Link DIR-820L. Happened feeding music from iPhone 6 and MacBook. I moved the iPhone close to routerno improvement. I did not try WiFI Direct Mode. ~~~ Comments & questions welcome ~~~

summary: Excellent so far
reviewText_clean: Ive had Bose QC25s which were decent but stopped working shortly after the warranty expired. Prior to that, I had Beats and those stopped working after a while too. So after being bitten by both aforementioned brands I decided to give Sennheiser a shot this time around (third times a charm, right?). These have already exceed my expectations in both terms of sound quality (which is superb), and NC works very well. I am pleasantly surprised. These are by far the best sounding headphones Ive ever used. I am traveling internationally soon and plan to use these during my long flights and I will update my review if theres anything relevant to add. If you're comparing these to Bose or Beats, do yourself a favor and go to go with Sennheiser, it is audiophile level sound quality which you won't find with the other two brands. FWIW: I considered the Sony MDR1000X2 but there were two major factors in me not going that route: 1) the headband cracking issue still seems to be an issue in the version 2. 2) Sony has capacitive touch. I need my headphones on flights where I can rest comfortably with a neck pillow and not have the headphones constantly freak out over every little touch. The PXC 550's have inductive touch which means only your fingers can affect the touch. This means a neck pillow touching the headphones won't cause it to pause or change songs etc. This was a crucial decision for me in going with Sennheiser. Also, if you check the Amazon reviews of the Sony headphones, they have lots of phony reviews which is pretty suspect; whereas the Sennheiser reviews are legit. Update: I used these on a long international flight. With noise cancellation on, they lasted a full 16 hours of flying time plus a two hour layover. Excellent and creates a sense of peace while you are on a noisy flight.

summary: which was working fine until I accidentally dropped it
reviewText_clean: I bought this camera to replace my Panasonic TZ3, which was working fine until I accidentally dropped it. I looked for a camera that is small enough to carry in my pocket like the TZ3. Because I often take pictures on the beach in bright sunlight I was looking for a camera with an EVF. After reviewing several cameras my options were the Panasonic DMC ZS40, DMC ZS50 and the Sony DSCHX90V. I chose for the Sony because of the pivoting LCD-monitor. To my surprise, the Sony DSCHX90V is almost identical in size as the TZ3. As odd as it may seem, I'm going to compare the Sony with my TZ3. Of course not technically but on quality and ergonomics. The TZ3 is sturdy and has round corners. It's easy to drop in it's pouch and then putting in- and taking out of your pocket. The Sony on the other hand although well built, has sharp corners, making it less "pocket-able". That's why I purchased the Sony LCJHWA/B Jacket Case to hang it around my neck. I have trouble too managing the buttons. They are small and almost flush to the body. Sometimes I have to push it more than once before it's activated. In darkness I even have trouble finding them, where as the buttons of TZ3 are rounded and are easy distinguishable. Now about the quality of the glass of the LCD-monitor. I have the Sony just a couple of months and it already got some scratches. The TZ3 on the other hand I have used extensively for many years, still there are no noticeable scratches on it's screen. So far the comparison between the two cameras. Now I want to elaborate about the pop-up viewfinder and pop-up flash. Although they are working fine, it takes extra time to get your camera ready for shooting, especially with the viewfinder. You first pop it up with one finger, but then I need two hands to pull out the eyepiece. Notwithstanding, the Sony DSCHX90V/B is a marvelous piece of technology with a quality lens to guarantee for making good photos or videos. But if I have to choose again I would opt for the (newer) Panasonic DMC-ZS60. For a couple of bucks more you even get 4K. But for me it's the ergonomics that count.

summary: Some units have a loud fan buzz, otherwise great
reviewText_clean: The unit works beautifully and I love the separation of LEDs from the connectors, but my first two units (of three) had a very loud buzzing noise in the fan. I'm not talking about the sound of moving air (which is of course expected, and is actually very quiet), but a persistent grinding/buzzing from the fan itself. The company's overseas support was of little help after approximately 80 pieces of mail back and forth. I sent recordings, and one person agreed it sounded "not right," then another said that it is normal. Another later added that "an engineer" said that they can't promise a replacement would be any better. Another said, "I know where you're coming from," and finally I was told that if I give them my credit card as "collateral" they will send me another one and "have your device tested in our facility." But there was no assurance at all that it would not be just as bad (in fact, I was essentially told it would be the same), so why give my plastic over the phone to someone at a distant call center who had never actually seen the product? I told them that I'll find a quiet fan and replace it myself if they can't do better than that. "It will void your warranty" was the only reply. UPDATE June 28, 2016: After lots of head-butting with non-tech support, I managed to connect with their US office... and they were very friendly and responsive, shipping a new unit without any difficulty. It did have the same issue but nowhere near as badly, with a sharp buzzing sound on top of the airflow noise itself (that part is fine and very quiet). The fan that is making the noise is a single EFB0412MD, and is 40x40x20mm, 3-wire. Mounting is trivial, with a standard connector over to the board.. so replacement should be easy. I bought a suitable fan, but the new unit has been so much better than the original one that I have not seen the need to do the replacement. At this point, I consider the problem solved, but have not yet stressed it with heavy POE loads. I just bumped my review up to four stars. (I did just bump it up to 3 stars, because other than the buzzing, it works perfectly and has a very sensible panel layout. Also, once I got past the overseas support and communicated with the home office in Silicon Valley, the quality of help went WAY up.)

summary: All in all, great board even to this day.
reviewText_clean: Great board, bad Boost button design...yet it didn't stop me from getting a Z270 Gaming M7 when the boost 'knob' went on me after almost 2 year's (and I rarely used it). I had a warranty on the board already, but I called MSI for troubleshooting and was told they would repair or replace the board without hesitation under the manufacturer's warranty. All in all, if I bought the next gen (and only went 270 to keep windows 7 or I would have got the latest), you can guess i'm still a satisfied customer. The product page for any MSI board give's you all the specific's, but BIOS Flashback is probably the best feature any board could have...honestly I would have still bought this today if my processor replacement (boost got stuck at 11...ouch) did not need to be a newer model and I wanted to keep my chipset up to date, I paid for the Z270 out of pocket because they didn't have any in stock where I had my replacement plan. Nuff said. If there's any con's to this board in my opinion aside from my boost knob breaking, i'd have to say it's kind of a pain to get it into the case (it went in two different one's from two different major company's, an they were around $200, 2ft by 2ft), it seem's to press against the PCI cover's every time, the power port's were always in the wrong place for my setup with a graphic's card (neither case was from MSI for the record, and the Z270 actually made it worse, unfortunately), but it ran like a dream with an I-7 6700K and 32 GB of RAM--without overclocking it I was able to actually play every PS3 game I tried, and even some PS4 game's on it with the Intel graphic's alone without any problem's before buying a graphic card. All in all, if your looking to go low budget or Windows 7 with on-board graphic's, this is def. a great choice...anything after this and your stuck with Win 10 or you need a graphic's card, at least on the Intel end of thing's, as the Z270 will still run the 6700K anyway's and that's the real issue, not the board. My three biggest complaint's are obviously the fact it broke, The location's of power connection's, some genius (this is actually in the manual) determined people were hanging a 20-40lb power supply on the roof of the case...right. Fired lol. The wiring layout in general is pretty horrible, as if they only took into account one area at a time and not a full build. The thing's that made me buy another, it's a beast, it has almost any port it's up to date with (probably why the wire setup is so bad) It's just plain sexy (another possible reason haha) After installing the board, I had zero complaint's until it broke... BIOS Flashback is the best idea since they invented the first BIOS (only took the computer world a million dead PC's from bad flashes to finally figure that out) Command Center should load your last save on boot, but it's great to keep an eye on and change all your setting's and has a voltage sensor that will alert you to anything including temp's. The BIOS has an auto shutdown for voltage too (that saved my entire build once) On-Board temp and error code's (although a more comprehensive list in the manual would be nice).

summary: Excellent FM, Below Average AM
reviewText_clean: This is a review of the Sangean DT-160 Short version: Excellent FM reception, below average AM reception. Operation of radio is not intuitive. Only 90 day warranty. Long version: I'm using this radio in the SF Bay Area. Outdoors: FM reception on this radio is its' strength. FM signals come in strong and lock on quickly, without interference from other stations. AM reception is the radios weakness, although the stations lock on quickly, most are faint and hard to hear. This is in a major metropolitan area! Indoors: FM reception drops to very good, AM reception is poor or non-existent, depending on the building. The radio is smaller than a deck of cards and feels lighter than the 2 AA batteries that power it. I had no problem turning the radio on, as it came on as I inserted the batteries. When I wanted to turn the radio off, I couldn't figure out how to do it. It turns out that the the band selector button doubles as the power button, although there is no lettering such as "power" on the radio. The enhanced bass feature works well. Owners manual is blissfully short and excellent. This radio has a 90 day warranty. Sony and panasonic radios have a 1 year warranty. I bought the "CL" version, the case is clear plastic and you can see the guts of the radio. Very interesting, I'd recommend this for a child so they can see all the parts, including the apparently delicate buttons. I did notice a small button battery that is soldered to the motherboard. I assume this is for power backup for your stations in the memory. Once this battery needs replacement, I hope it doesn't affect the basic operation of the radio, as this battery is not user replaceable. A technician skilled in soldering might be able to replace it, but definitely not the average person. I used a pair of Panasonic earbuds and Philips headphones to test this radio. With the Philips headphones, some of stations seemed to come in stronger and there was less background "hiss" than with the Panasonic earbuds. Try different headphones & earbuds to see which works best for you. If you need a FM pocket radio, this is it. If you need an AM radio outdoors, this may work. If you need AM indoors, look for another radio. summary: Possibly the best overall mid-size Bluetooth speaker available everywhere.
reviewText_clean: I gotta say My early impressions are quite positive with the speaker. From the way it's packaged to the button layout to the sound quality, it's about as good compact Bluetooth speaker as I think you'll find at this price point. It appears to be well built and if the battery holds out, this will give many good years of service. I'd come into the market for a compact, splash-proof Bluetooth speaker after my last one, a TDK A33, started experiencing charging issues and I was unable to source a replacement battery. It sets the benchmark for sound quality at this general size level of speakers, with deep thumping bass and the ability to produce crisp and clean highs with the use of an EQ (out of the box, it's actually rather muddy but not for lack of ability.) After a short-lived experiment with a smaller Altec Lansing that died *just* out of warranty, I set my eyes on this model because of its form factor and ratings. From the get-go JBL does a good job with first impressions. The box it ships in well made and almost too nice for such an inexpensive speaker. The instructions are simple and to the point, and it includes a USB charging cable, but no wall wart. You'll need to plug up to a computer USB port or use a third party micro USB charger if you want to charge it from a wall outlet. Setup was a breeze and it paired successfully with my ancient Android tablet in seconds. Of note is that there is a row of white dot lights below the power and share buttons that indicates battery level. As far as I can tell, when charging, the top light never burns continuously; it flashes like it's always charging, even when it's done. Kind of odd. But anytime during use that you press a button, those lights will shine showing the relative battery level. My early experiences with it indicate it'll run approximately 4-5 hours on a single charge at moderate volume levels. The range on Bluetooth is also quite good. I was able to move a good 40 feet away with multiple walls in between my device(s) and the speaker with minimal dropouts. My biggest worry with this speaker was the tube shape. It doesn't say anywhere whether it has any kind of padding or footing to keep it from rolling off a ledge. My main use place is in the shower on a dry, narrow ledge. Luckily, it has a rather invisible but useful indentation when operating on its side. If the JBL logo is facing you, at a slightly upward-facing angle, it will rest without rolling away even on slightly imperfect surfaces. It can also stand on end, and the down-facing side speaker still can be heard thanks to tiny undulations in the molding, allowing sound to escape. It's a thoughtful touch, but it still sounds best on its side. You won't hear much in the way of stereo separation from this small of a speaker but it will still fill a small room with sound and do so somewhat faithfully to the source material. Obviously, bass is lacking due to the overall side of this device, but careful placement in a corner or near a wall allows it to resonate better. It does not come anywhere close to the deep, downright rich and punchy bass of the TDK, instead sounding a bit more plastic-y and muddy, but I don't think it'll be an issue for most people, unless you are in love with bass-heavy music. I would definitely worry about blowing out those side "woofers" either from the volume being too high or from something hitting them, as they're completely exposed. This device isn't waterproof but it appears to be well sealed for splash proof duty. I've been using it in the shower where it does not come in direct contact with running water, but I've splashed it a little bit and used wet fingers to change the volume and so far, so good. The plastic/rubber door that seals the aux in and charging jacks is thick and tight fitting. Any water that gets on the speaker grille fabric beads up and does not soak in, which is nice. It's easy to dry as most of the water just drips off. The power and share buttons are flat, but the volume, phone and Bluetooth buttons are raised and tactile, which makes for easy hands free use in many situations. Additional features are the ability to share (via the share button with what appears to be an hourglass-like glyph on it) and get firmware upgrades. It has two sharing modes, letting two JBL speakers act as independent left and right channels, or in a party mode that plays the same music equally over multiple devices. I didn't test this out. It's a bit gimmicky but I don't know many other speakers that can do this. It appears to be well built and if the battery holds out, this will give many good years of service. I'd come into the market for a compact, splash-proof Bluetooth speaker after my last one, a TDK A33, started experiencing charging issues and I was unable to source a replacement battery. From the get-go JBL does a good job with first impressions. The box it ships in well made and almost too nice for such an inexpensive speaker. The instructions are simple and to the point, and it includes a USB charging cable, but no wall wart. You'll need to plug up to a computer USB port or use a third party micro USB charger if you want to charge it from a wall outlet. As far as I can tell, when charging, the top light never burns continuously; it flashes like it's always charging, even when it's done. Kind of odd. summary: If you're into setting up flashy LED patterns you'll love this keyboard
reviewText_clean: Packaged well; comes with keycap puller, magnetic wrist-rest, a couple of "viper" stickers and a small Quick Start Guide card (very basic). I'd already downloaded the latest driver/setup v. 2.4 from Patriot's webpage, but it works when you plug it in and - if I remember right - my default LED pattern was rainbow wave. Anyway, you still need to run the setup to update the firmware and configure any color patterns you want. Once you do this it comes up with the usual install prompts and installs the Patriot Viper Keyboard app on your desktop; running that (for me) brought up a prompt that I needed to update the driver (?); did it anyway, going through the steps. I will say that at one point I did have to reset the keyboard - Viper key+Pause Break for about 5 seconds - but it all ran okay after that. Pros: If you're into setting up flashy LED patterns you'll love this keyboard. It's programmable, including options to turn gaming mode and the Windows key off or on in the software, as well as setting up different profiles. Has the USB pass-through, a really nicely braided cable, and comes with a 2 year warranty, which I like because my last one only had a 1 year. Not-so-pro: I'm trying to get used to these kailh switches coming from using a (now dead) keyboard that had Cherry MX brown switches. Have to say I prefer the Cherry ones with the definitive tactile response. To be fair though, that kb was another $30 more. Just need to get used to these I guess. The other thing is a minor ergonomic note - even with the legs extended on the keyboard, you get a minimal height boost at the back. If that makes any difference to you. The reason I mention it is because, even with the wrist-rest, the front of the keyboard feels a bit higher than I'm used to. But then I was using a foam wrist pad prior and that's probably the difference. Just an observation. Overall I think that it's worth the price so far. If it had the Cherry switches I'd be more than satisfied.

summary: You can't believe how good this is!
reviewText_clean: I am unlucky enough to be a discriminating hifi aficionado on a shoe string budget. I have, over the years, been able to obtain some very good equipment by buying older models of the good stuff, knowing they were built to very high standards and designed to last. In that way, I was able to purchase Klipshorn speakers and had a McIntosh amp and preamp that really sounded good together. I had the misfortune of an electrical storm that took out my McIntosh items due to my not realizing they were not being protected by my quick blow circuit protectors and the cost to repair them was more than I had paid for them in the first place. While jealously reviewing the tube equipment available from Mc or Fisher or Marantz etc, I came across the Yaqin MC-13S and was surprised at the price for a 45 watt per channel integrated all tube amp and then I read the reviews. Wow! I thought this was worth taking a chance on, so I did. It only took about 8 days to arrive from Hong Kong (shipping included in the price!), well packed and beautiful. I had also purchased a line conditioner as I live in the country and wanted to make sure to protect the product and the sound as well as I could. After installing the 8 tubes and adjusting the bias (all you need is a good volt meter but they were already factory adjusted and marked at to which slot each marked tube was supposed to go in to match the factory adjusting, I just wanted to be more hands on), I hooked up the klipshorns and gave it a go. Now the thing about tubes is that they have a break in period before they settle into the final smoothed out sound that you will get from then on. The break in period is discussed as anywhere from 25 to 100 hours, depending on what you read. The sound I got when I first played Yanni's Tribute album was better than my Mc stuff had ever been, with no break-in at all. I could not believe the richness of the sound of that orchestra. Then I tried my second favorite thing to listen to - clear, pure voices. I listened to a mix that I made that the only thing the songs had in common was the power of the voice and I had ballads by Don Williams, Celine, Josh Groban, Johnny Mathis, Roger Whitaker, Micky Newbury, Mary Travers etc. I just listened and listened to the wee hours of the morning. I was stunned by the purity of the sound I got from this amp and those speakers. Most of you reading this are not in the category that looks for 1000 watt amps, you know what a class A tube amp can do and the 45 watts is a lot - a whole lot - of power that will drive good speakers very well. I really think you should seriously consider giving this amp a try. For some reason, I get a catalog every month from an esoteric hifi company that actually has speaker cables that cost $7000 and amps and turntables that costs as much as a good used mercedes, but that equipment could not make me one bit more pleased than this very inexpensive but very classy amp. It comes with a 1 year warranty and I added a 4 year extension for about $40. I tried tube rolling just for the heck of it, but put the originals back in, they are perfect. I also did have occasion to contact the company about a minor issue (warranty card was not in the box). The customer support was instantaneous and very cooperative. You ever have anything that you liked it so much you were tempted to buy another one just so you have a spare? That's how much I like this! Very pleased customer!

reviewText_clean: This is an AMAZING speaker! Build quality and sound quality are excellent. We are a family of three. We go TV free on the weekend so music,podcasts and audiobooks are our main source of entertainment. We were using an older system that docked to an iPod. The Raumfeld One M speaker has brought so much joy and entertainment to our lives. If your looking to get back into your music collection or want to enjoy radio shows this system is perfect. EVERYTHING sounds BETTER played through this system. We have a three bedroom ranch. We placed the speaker in the living room. We can hear it all through the house. The sound is rich and clear with NO distortions. You can use the app to tweak it to your liking. We have found the out of the box setting almost perfect for our needs. I may try toning down the bass a little. This system can get very loud if desired. I can feel it vibrate the floor and walls but the sound does NOT distort. Amazon packs this system very securely. It was double boxed. The inner Raumfeld box is tightly packed with cushioning foam. We selected the White system. It's beautiful ! It looks very modern and high end. The unit is quite heavy. You can see and feel this is a quality product. We had a few issues setting this up. This system has app that you download to your phone or tablet. The app is the controller for this system. There are preset buttons on the front of the unit but we have not been able to figure out how to configure them yet. I believe another review mentions this same issue. There is a volume control knob on the front off the unit. The app can be acquired through the Apple app store or the google play store. We downloaded the app to an android phone but we were unable to connect to the system. We next tried our IPad...Success! * They include a high quality Lan cord to connect directly to your router if needed. It Connected almost instantly to our IPad. The app is fairly intuitive. We played with it and were able to figure things out. I have NO music stored on the IPad. It was searching in the my music file. I tried to play podcasts I had stored in the Icatcher app I was not able to play those. I am not sure if you can play items that are NOT stored in the my music file. I have to play with this more and I will update my review. We attached an IPod nano with the line in feature. You can only control the IPod nano through the Raumfeld app. Luckily it works perfectly ! We also attached a music filled thumb drive through the USB port and pulled it up in the app. Again it worked flawlessly ! We next tried the Tunein option. This is my favorite ! With Tunein you can get pretty much any radio station or listen to podcasts. There is a Spotify tab too but I don't use Spotify. I am pretty sure you already know this but this system is WIFI only there is no Bluetooth option. My only concern regarding this system is they provided very little documentation. The website offers only slightly more infomation. It was pretty easy to figure out but one would think at this price point the instructions would be clearer. In closing the system is fantastic sounding and a wonderful addition to our home. We are enjoying discovering all of its capabilities. * Warranty is two years and unit must have been purchased directly from Berlin Acoustics or an Authorized seller. * While I was exploring the Raumfeld website I noticed in the FAQ section a mention that Raumfeld allows you to try this system in your home for a number of weeks. It mentions it will take it back if it does not meet your needs and offer a full refund. Again I saw this on the Raumfeld site NOT Amazon's site. If this interests you perhaps check out their website for further information.
